title: Phase 1–2 · platform and engines
detail: Tenancy, identity, audit hash chain, config resolution, Money; then SPX, the rule/formula/workflow engines and their conformance corpus.

title: Phase 3 · People
detail: 32 authoring types, 13 surfaces, the ten-stage write pipeline, encryption and checksums. A field is added with zero code files touched.

title: Phase 4 · Time and absence
detail: One is_weekly_off(). The attendance day as a window labelled by the shift start — cross-midnight is ONE day. Comp-off end to end.

title: Phase 5 · Compensation
detail: Prorate the gross ONCE then split; the balance component absorbs the residue. Reconciliation aborts a run on one paisa of drift.

title: Phase 6 · Statutory framework
detail: Ed25519 signed rule packs, JCS canonicalisation, immutable store, applicability, the floor, the obligation calendar and returns. BLOCKED on the compliance-owner appointment for content.

title: Phase 7 · Compliance and the collections pack
detail: ONE compliance_status(). The three absent-record states, none returning valid. The collections vertical installs as data with no PHP.

title: Phase 8–10 · Reports, operations, migration
detail: Runtime report columns, delivered-only-on-acknowledgement, redaction into the log; no default credential, rollback of code AND schema, verified restore drills; the Class C tolerance policy.

title: Phase 0–2 gates, definition of done, traceability
detail: The earliest phases had no gate at all. Phase 0 is BLOCKED: 83 Tier 1 decisions unanswered. Traceability says 195 of 3,313 requirements are checked.

title: Part XXIV · the /api/v3 contract
detail: URL grammar linter, closed error catalogue, idempotency in the domain transaction, cursor pagination. Then OpenAPI generation and the three blocking contract gates.

title: Part XXIV · the webhook engine
detail: Signature over timestamp AND nonce, transport-layer replay guard, full-jitter retry, and nothing dropped silently.

title: The console becomes viewable
detail: Thirteen pages over the real engines: build status, payroll, attendance, statutory, compliance, API. No composer, no vendor, no database.

title: The application exists — public/app.php
detail: Sign in, an employments list you can add to, and a payslip computed by Platform\Payroll. No composer, no vendor, no database. No default credential: first run issues a one-time enrolment token.

title: Gates refused src/App — moved to surface/
detail: The enforcement toolchain rejected the demo shell for reaching into Platform internals and not being a declared module. It was right: the shell moved OUT of src/ rather than the gate being exempted.

title: Authorisation through the real decider
detail: Every action asks Platform\Access\AccessDecider. A viewer sees no Run payroll link, no Add form, and a POST attempt is refused SERVER-SIDE with the decider's own reason — hiding a button is not authorisation.

title: Attendance capture, wired to payroll
detail: Record punches; Platform\Attendance settles them. A 22:00–06:00 night is ONE day (495m worked, 2m late, 15m overtime); the same punches under a day shift split into two incomplete days. Payable days are DERIVED and carried into the payslip.

title: Leave requests and an as-at balance
detail: Request → approve → the ledger takes a debit that NAMES the request. A rejection never touches the ledger. The balance is SUM(credits)-SUM(debits) at the date asked about, so approved future leave shows today's figure AND the figure after it.

title: Attendance + leave → payable days → payslip
detail: One figure, derived in one place: worked days + PAID leave. Unpaid leave is not payable (the C-LOP defect). A day both worked and on leave counts ONCE and is REPORTED rather than resolved silently — only a person knows which record is the mistake.

title: The audit trail, hash-chained
detail: surface/Trail.php records employment.created, attendance.punch.recorded, leave.requested and leave.decided into a hash chain (Platform\Audit\HashChain). ?r=trail shows before to after values and verifies the chain. Probed live: editing a reason in place, deleting a row and reordering two rows are each detected with a distinct reason; restoring the file verifies again. Passwords, secrets, tokens and hashes are redacted out of recorded values. Gates 13/0, tests 4400 assertions 0 failures.

title: The salary structure moved out of code
detail: structure() returned four hand-written new SalaryComponent() calls — the first law broken in the most ordinary way, since an HRA percentage is a business decision. Components now come from config/salary-structure.json plus versions published at ?r=structure, through surface/Structure.php. Versions are effective-dated and append-only: publishing never overwrites, so a March payslip reprints against the March structure. Proven: publishing a 55 percent basic effective 2026-09-01 changes the payslip from 25,000 to 27,500 with no code change, while 2026-08-31 still computes 25,000. Refusals at publish time, not run time: a duplicate effective date, a malformed date, non-JSON, and a percent_of with no base. Permissions payroll.structure.view/publish come from the real catalogue; publishing is audited into the hash chain. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: The payroll register — a month, not a payslip
detail: surface/Register.php closes a period across every employment: payable days derived per employment from punches and approved leave, one control total, and the run stored with its inputs, the structure version it used, and a fingerprint of every figure on every line. verify() recomputes from those stored inputs and compares to the paisa, so reproducibility is TESTED on every page load rather than claimed. Probed non-vacuously: a tampered fingerprint reports NOT REPRODUCED, a missing structure version reports that it cannot be reproduced rather than diffing against the current structure, and an unclosed period says so. A closed period is refused a second close. Employments with an unpaired punch, an overlap or loss of pay are listed WITH the reason and paid for the days they can account for, never dropped from the run. Closing is audited into the hash chain. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: The leave policy moved out of code
detail: The paid-type list ['EL','CL','SL'] was a constant in Surface\\PayrollPeriod and the opening balance 18 was a literal in the front controller — both are policy. config/leave-policy.json now declares each type: paid or unpaid, opening days, monthly accrual, cap. Payroll reads the SAME paid list the leave screen shows, so the two cannot disagree about whether a day was paid. Accrual is POSTED to the ledger one entry per month, not computed by multiplying months by a rate: a posted entry can be read, explained and adjusted, and does not change retrospectively when the rate does. Each posting names itself (accrual:EL:2026-03), so the leave page accrues on load and is safe to refresh — probed: 11 entries after the first load, still 11 after three refreshes. The cap stops accrual without truncating what is earned — probed: an employment joined 2019-01-01 posts 30 accruals and stops at exactly 45. A missing policy file and an unknown type are refusals, not defaults, because both would silently make a day unpaid. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: Statutory contributions on the payslip
detail: surface/Statutory.php loads the Phase 6 synthetic pack through the real PackVerifier (Ed25519 signature and countersignature, JCS canonicalisation, platform-version compatibility) into the immutable PackStore, declares applicability with a reason AND evidence, and computes through StatutoryEngine. The payslip now shows the contribution with its rule code, pack version, content hash and source reference — re-derivable, not a claim. The wage base is assembled from the DECLARED FLAG the rule names: is_synth_base was added to C-BASIC in config/salary-structure.json, not to any PHP file, which is the point — a statutory scheme this build has not met is a flag somebody adds. The pack stays SYNTHETIC and every figure carries the synthetic stamp: Phase 6 is blocked on a named compliance owner, and typing real PF and ESI rates in to make the page look finished is exactly the failure the blueprint names. Two presentation bugs of my own were caught by testing rather than by reading: a missing platform-version argument surfaced as a REFUSED pack (correct behaviour, wrong cause), and worse, a not-applicable row rendered as an amount of 0.00 — a silent zero, the precise failure this subsystem exists to prevent. It now reads NOT DETERMINED and says it is not a zero deduction. Computed 700.00 on a base of 30,000.00 at 2026-10-31, matching golden case SYN-01. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0; the Phase 6 exit gate still reports 4 of 5 with 1 NOT PROVEN, blocked, unchanged.

title: What the employee sees
detail: A read-only ?r=me view for the person being paid. The payslip is read back from the CLOSED RUN, never recomputed for the screen: a payslip that recomputes on view can disagree with the one that was paid, and the employee is the last person who should discover that. Each line carries the engine's own working rather than a total to be taken on trust. Concerns recorded against the run — days needing regularisation, a leave overlap, loss of pay — are shown to the EMPLOYEE too, not only to the payroll officer; a deduction whose reason the person cannot see is a payroll query somebody answers by hand. Leave balances are shown per type with the policy basis beside them, and the full ledger is on the page — every accrual and every debit — because a balance nobody can take apart is a balance that gets disputed and then settled by exporting a spreadsheet. Verified live: with no closed period the page says so rather than showing an empty payslip of zero; after closing, the balance reads 12 days at 2026-09-05 rather than 13.5, because the September accrual is effective 2026-09-30 and the ledger is asked as at today — the effective-dating working exactly as intended. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: Correcting a closed month
detail: close() refuses a second run, but no on its own is not an answer: a payroll officer who has just found a missing punch needs somewhere to go, and a system that offers nothing gets the database edited instead. Register::correct() recomputes the month from what the records say today — through the SAME private computeMonth() that close() uses, so a correction cannot quietly differ in method — and stores the DIFFERENCE per employment alongside the untouched original, with a reason somebody typed and both fingerprints kept. The difference is the product, not the new total: what was paid is history, what is owed is the only figure anyone acts on, and that is exactly what an overwrite destroys. A correction that changes nothing is still recorded, because we checked and it was right is an answer worth keeping. Probed end to end: no reason is refused; an unclosed period is refused; a recompute with no change reports NOTHING CHANGED; adding a missing punch produces a net difference of 2,000.00 while the original stays at 1,800.00. The branch most easily lost is covered — an employment paid in the original and absent from the recomputation is found by walking the ORIGINAL too, since nothing in the new run points at it. Two of my own errors were caught in the process: deriving net by adding up line kinds would have treated an employer contribution as a deduction, so the row now stores the engine's own net; and a delta message asserted money owed when the figure was negative. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: The calendar, the shift and regularisation
detail: Three at once. (1) config/calendar.json: weekly offs, holidays, the shift and the PRORATION BASIS. The basis is declared and never defaulted — calendar days and working days give different payslips for the same month and the same attendance, and a platform that picks one silently has made a business decision for the customer without telling them; a config that does not say is refused. A holiday falling on a weekly off counts once — probed: August 2026 has 21 working days, not 20, because 15 August is a Saturday. (2) Every hardcoded 09:00 and 18:00 is gone from public/app.php; the count is now zero. PayrollPeriod's Monday-to-Friday private static working-day count is replaced by the calendar. (3) surface/Regularisation.php gives a day the register refuses to pay a way out, or somebody edits the punch table. An approval ADDS a punch with source=regularised carrying the request id; the device's own punch is never edited, so the reader missed the exit and the exit time was changed stay distinguishable in a dispute. A rejection adds nothing at all — not a zero-minute punch, not a cancelled one — and the day keeps reporting itself unresolved. Requested and decided are two acts; that one role can do both in this build is a stated ceiling, not a silent one. Probed live: no reason refused, duplicate pending request refused, deciding twice refused, and a day going from 1 unpaired to clean with both punches visible and only the second marked regularised. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: Arrears, the bank advice, and full and final
detail: Three. (1) ARREARS: a correction against an earlier month is carried into the next close as an arrears line and only then marked settled — an unsettled difference that never reaches a payslip is a report that agrees with itself and pays nobody. The month's net and the arrears are kept separate AND summed, because what did this month cost and what did we still owe are both asked. Probed: 1,935.49 carried into September, settled_in recorded, and October carries nothing. (2) BANK ADVICE: the point where a payroll stops being a report. An employment with no bank details does not fall out of a filter — the advice REFUSES and names them, because a file that pays 47 of 48 people balances perfectly against its own total and is wrong. The control total is checked against the RUN, not recomputed from the rows just written; summing a file and comparing it to itself proves the addition, which was never in doubt. Probed non-vacuously: a tampered declared total is refused. A negative net is excluded from the credit and LISTED as a recovery. One real bug caught: the arrears column carried a formatted amount, and one thousands separator inside a CSV field shifts every column after it — a bank file that fails quietly. (3) FULL AND FINAL: an exit is not a delete. Quoted first and recorded second with a person reading it in between, which is the only control that catches a wrong last working day, since every figure is correct arithmetic on the date it was given. Encashment uses the balance ON THE EXIT DATE, and recording DEBITS the ledger so nobody is paid twice. My own modelling error, caught by reading the output: I encashed every PAID type, producing 72,000 of encashment on a 60,000 salary. Paid and encashable are different questions — sick leave is paid when taken and is not a sum owed on exit. It is now an encashable flag in the leave policy, declared, not assumed. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: Tenancy and the approval a payment waits for
detail: (1) TENANCY IS STRUCTURAL. Store gains forTenant(); every read filters and every write stamps, so a screen cannot forget the where-clause — and the list is of PLATFORM-scoped collections (tenants, users), so a NEW collection is tenant-scoped by DEFAULT. An allow-list of scoped tables leaks through whichever one somebody forgets to add, which is the SmartPRS 2 finding: rows with a NULL tenant_id visible to everybody. Another tenant's row is NOT FOUND rather than forbidden, because forbidden confirms the id exists. Writing another tenant's id is refused rather than re-stamped: moving a row between tenants silently cannot be undone by fixing a filter afterwards. Probed: A sees 1 and B sees 0 of the same file; B's write does not disturb A; B cannot find, overwrite or wipe A's rows. (2) APPROVAL. A closed run is computed but not payable. The person who closed it CANNOT approve it — refused, not warned, because the control exists exactly for the case where one person is in a hurry, and whoever built a figure is worst placed to notice it is wrong. BankAdvice refuses an unapproved run outright: a bank file produced before the approval is a payment nobody authorised, and the bank cannot tell the difference. Probed with two real users: self-approval refused, second person approves, advice then generates, second approval refused. (3) A bug of mine, caught by running it: the write() guard I added to protect other tenants broke put(), which legitimately writes the merged raw collection, and separately the hash-chained trail. put() and the trail now go through an internal writer; the trail appends per row, which also makes the audit chain per-tenant, which is what it should have been. Gates 13/0, tests 4400/0.

title: The schema port, and what the spine caught
detail: 88 business tables ported from SmartPRS 2 into real MySQL migrations, captured by EXECUTING SmartPRS 2's migrations against a recording stub rather than parsing them — their filenames lie about their contents. SmartPRS 2 was read only throughout; files were copied out, nothing written. 246 corrections recorded, none applied silently: tenant_id NOT NULL with a RESTRICT foreign key on all 85 tenant tables (SmartPRS 2 declares it nullable in 43 places and has 5 FKs in the whole 96-table schema); company_id renamed employer_company_id so it can never be mistaken for tenancy; 33 enums and 39 free-string statuses moved to the published vocabulary; DATETIME to DATE on every _on column. SmartPRS 3's own checks caught five things I got wrong, which is the whole reason they exist: a foreign key with no ON DELETE behaviour; TIMESTAMP instead of DATETIME for created_at; Schema::create outside database/migrations; a variable table name the tenancy gate could not read statically; and worst, money as integer paise — a correction I applied from first principles without checking that SmartPRS 3's foundation and its Money value object already agree on DECIMAL(18,4) read as a string. Two money representations in one schema is worse than either, so the established convention won. The generated isolation suite now proves 117 tenant-scoped tables rather than 32; three port tables had no writable text column, and the fix was to widen the accepted types rather than lower the expected count, because a table quietly dropped from an isolation suite is a table nobody is checking. Gates 13/0, tests 5495 assertions 0 failures.

title: The repository over the ported tables
detail: surface/SqlStore.php has the same shape as Store — all(), find(), put(), forTenant() — backed by MySQL, so screens move across one at a time without changing a caller. Tenancy is structural in SQL now: every read carries WHERE tenant_id = ? and every write carries the value, and no screen builds a query so none can forget. The platform-scoped list is Store's own constant rather than a second copy, so the two cannot drift. Another tenant's row is NOT FOUND rather than forbidden, because forbidden confirms the id exists. Table and column names are checked against information_schema rather than escaped — an identifier cannot be a bound parameter, so checking is the only safe thing to do with one — and the column list is read from the database rather than kept in a map, because a map is a second description of the schema that goes stale on the first migration that lands without it. A column the table does not have is refused rather than dropped: a field that appears to save and does not is discovered months later by whoever needed it. write() does not exist at all. One thing improved after probing: B writing A's row id worked out correctly but only via a raw duplicate-key error — the right outcome reached by accident and explained badly — so the ownership check is now explicit and by name. tests/sql_store_test.php proves all of it against a real database, asserting the message TEXT rather than the exception class, because a refusal whose text stops explaining itself is one nobody can act on. Non-vacuity probed: breaking the cross-tenant guard, the unknown-column guard and the identifier check each makes the suite fail, and restoring each returns it to clean. Gates 13/0, tests 5510 assertions 0 failures across 53 files.

title: Onto the database, and Law 2 enforced by the gate
detail: RowStore is now the contract both stores implement, so every surface class hints the interface and switching storage is configuration rather than an edit to eight files. Database.php decides between MySQL and JSON files and carries the REASON to the screen — an application that silently falls back to file storage is one where somebody enters a month of payroll into the wrong thing and finds out later. Every outcome names itself: no .env, no DB_DATABASE, unreachable, reachable but empty, connected. It never creates the database and never migrates on boot: a page load that alters a live schema is how a bad deploy becomes a data loss. Six new tables for concepts SmartPRS 2 has no equivalent for — enrolment, leave_entries, payroll_corrections, structures, settlements, audit — each with its reason written above it; where SmartPRS 2 already has the concept the surface was pointed at ITS table (employments to employees, punches to attendance_logs, leave_requests to leaves, regularisations to attendance_corrections), because two homes for the same data is the defect being removed, not one to introduce. 128 tables now apply cleanly to real MySQL. The db-privilege gate then failed on my own .env: the app was running as root, which holds DDL on everything and UPDATE on the append-only tables. That is Law 2 and the gate exists for exactly this. tools/db/grant-application-account.php now issues per-TABLE grants — per-table because a database-level grant covers tables that do not exist yet, including the append-only one somebody adds next month, which would arrive writable. It reads the append-only list from the GATE's own constant rather than repeating it, because two copies of a privilege list is one copy that goes stale and the stale one is always the one in force. It refuses to run against root, since granting root exactly what it needs is a no-op that looks like it worked. audit, payroll_corrections and settlements were added to the append-only list: the hash chain makes an edit detectable, and an account holding UPDATE defeats exactly that detection. Probed for real: CREATE, UPDATE on audit and DELETE on settlements are all denied to the application account, while ordinary reads and writes still work. Gates 13/0, tests 5583 assertions 0 failures.

title: Customising a module without writing code
detail: Each of the 79 modules can now declare a fields block in config/modules.json: label, type, options, required, readonly, hidden, help. Types are DERIVED from the column when nothing is declared — a date column gets a date picker, a tinyint a checkbox, a text a textarea — so every module is usable the moment its table exists with no per-module work; the declaration is the customisation on top. Declaring fields also CHOOSES them: employees has 81 columns, and a form offering all of them is not a customised screen but a database browser, so a module that declares fields shows exactly those in the declared order while one that declares none shows everything. Rules are enforced BEFORE storage so the message names the field in the customer's words rather than the column in MySQL's — probed live: a missing required field says Employee code is required, and a value outside a declared option list says Status must be one of active, probation, notice, exited, suspended, got on-holiday. A declared key naming a column the table does not have is reported ON THE SCREEN — a customisation that quietly does nothing is worse than one that fails, because whoever wrote it believes it took; probed with a deliberately wrong key, which the screen named. columnsOf() moved onto the RowStore contract because a form derived from the first row is a screen that only works once it already has data, which is the one moment it is no use. uuid joined id as store-owned: it is identity, not a field, and offering it invites a value that breaks a unique index. Worked example committed for employees (17 fields with real Indian payroll vocabulary — PT state, UAN, PAN, PF and ESI applicability) and leaves. Gates 13/0, tests 5583 assertions 0 failures.

title: The customisation surface, finished
detail: config/modules.json now carries everything a module needs to differ from the default, and none of it is code. Per FIELD: label, type, options, required, readonly, hidden, help — and LOOKUP, which points a column at another table and shows names instead of ids in BOTH the form and the list. employee_id showing 47 is a screen that makes somebody open a second one to find out who 47 is. The lookup is declared rather than guessed from the column name, because reporting_manager_id points at employees and no naming convention gets that right. The option list is read THROUGH THE TENANT-SCOPED STORE, because a dropdown is the easiest place in an application to leak another customer's names. An id that points at nothing is refused by name: Department, there is no record with id 9999 to point at. Per MODULE: permissions {view, edit}. Can see the employee list and can see everybody's salary are not the same permission, and giving them one name is how the second gets granted by somebody who meant the first — proven by role, where a viewer sees employees and is refused payroll runs. 79 modules, 18 with declared fields and lookups, 25 with their own permissions; the rest fall back to derived types and the default permission, which is what makes them usable before anybody has customised them. Gates 13/0, tests 5583 assertions 0 failures.

title: Every module speaks the customer's vocabulary
detail: All 79 modules now carry field declarations: 371 fields, 44 dropdowns, 22 cross-table lookups, 38 required rules, 25 with their own permissions. The vocabularies are declared PER MODULE rather than shared, because status means five different things across these tables and one common list would be wrong on four of them — a loan is requested, approved, disbursed, recovering, closed or written off; a complaint is received, under review, substantiated, unsubstantiated or closed; an invoice is draft, issued, part paid, paid, overdue or cancelled. A bug of my own, caught by opening a screen rather than by reading the config: the generator skipped any module that already had a fields block, so the 17 modules given a lookup in the previous pass kept that one field and lost every other — Loans showed a single Employee dropdown and nothing else. Skipping was meant to protect hand-written declarations from being overwritten; merging does that AND fills the rest, which is what it should have done. Audited afterwards against the live schema: 371 fields, zero declared columns that do not exist, zero modules with an empty form, and every one of the 79 pages loading without error. Gates 13/0, tests 5583 assertions 0 failures.

title: Reports and the dashboard
detail: config/reports.json declares 16 reports across People, Cost, Leave and attendance, Statutory, Payroll and Off-roll: table, group_by, measure, column, an optional lookup that turns grouping keys into names, and a where clause. Reports runs them. A new report is an entry in that file; SmartPRS 2 answers each report from its own controller, so a change to how a total is formatted has to be made in every one. Aggregation happens in PHP over rows the TENANT-SCOPED store returned, not in a GROUP BY composed from the declaration — a declaration file that builds SQL can reach any table by any path, and a report is exactly the feature somebody adds in a hurry. Every report states how many rows it counted, because a total from an unknown number of rows is a figure nobody can check and out of how many is the first question anyone asks. Rows that cannot be grouped are counted and shown as (not set) rather than dropped: a hundred employees with no department quietly missing from a headcount by department gives a report that balances perfectly and is wrong. The dashboard runs the SAME reports rather than its own queries, so the two can never disagree about a number. Verified against real data: Operations 12,60,000 and Finance 16,80,000 and unassigned 6,00,000 summing to 35,40,000 with the exited employee correctly excluded by the report's own filter, and all 16 reports running clean. A real bug surfaced because MySQL had stopped and the app fell back to files exactly as designed: on an empty collection the file store reports no columns, so the form had no fields and the first row could never be added — the screen only works once it already has data, which is the one moment it is no use. My fallback fired on an exception but not on an empty result; it now falls back to the module's own declaration, which exists before any data does. Gates 13/0, tests 5583 assertions 0 failures.

title: Requests and approvals, declared
detail: config/workflows.json declares five chains — leave, expense, advance, regularisation, increment — each naming its subject, its steps, who decides, the comment rule per step, an SLA, and the amount at which another approver joins. SmartPRS 2 answers these screens from a 108 KB controller where every chain is written out in PHP, so a customer wanting one more signature above 50,000 needs a release; here it is a number in a file. Proven live with two real users: 3 days waits on the manager alone, 12 days pulls HR in, and 75,000 pulls in manager then finance then director — all from thresholds, no code. SELF-APPROVAL IS REFUSED at the decision, not merely hidden in the inbox: a hidden button is a UI convention and an API call walks straight past one. A step that does not apply is shown WITH ITS REASON rather than removed — skipped, 3 day(s) is not over the 10 day(s) threshold — because routing by amount means the chain differs per request and somebody looking at an approved claim needs to know whether finance saw it or whether the amount put it under their threshold; a missing row answers nothing. A reason is required where the step declares it, refused by the step's own label. Decisions are APPENDED, never overwriting the last, so a step rejected and later re-approved shows both: who approved this, and had anyone rejected it first, is the question asked when something has gone wrong. A rejection ends the chain rather than carrying on to the next approver — a question nobody needed answered. workflow_decisions is append-only at the DATABASE grant, because a decision that can be rewritten is not a record of who decided. The inbox separates what is waiting on you from what you raised and are waiting on: a list that mixes the two is a list nobody trusts. Gates 13/0, tests 5611 assertions 0 failures.

title: The 39 tables that were not in any migration
detail: My first port was wrong and this is the correction. It covered 88 tables; SmartPRS 2 has 127. The other 39 are created by Schema::create() INSIDE controllers and services — 60 such calls across 40 files — so a migration-only reading cannot find them, and mine did not. I found it by trying to build the recruitment module and discovering that recruitment, job_openings and interviews do not exist in the captured schema: the largest module in the system, 32 routes, backed by tables nothing declares. That is the second law broken at its root — a page load can create a table, so two installations used differently have different schemas with no record of why. Extracted every runtime Schema::create block by brace-matching, re-emitted them as one migration, and PROVED the extraction by applying it to real MySQL rather than by trusting the regex: 169 tables, zero failures. 43 further corrections, including two the spine caught that I had not thought to look for. A unique index that did not lead with tenant_id: unique(emp_code, log_date) means two tenants cannot both have an employee E001 on the same day, and one customer's data silently blocking another's is the worst way for a tenancy defect to surface because it looks like a validation error and gets fixed by renaming the employee. And three money precisions for one kind of number — decimal(12,2) and (14,2) in the runtime tables against (18,4) in the migrations, so the same rupee rounds differently depending on which table it passes through. Two bugs of my own on the way: a tenancy-column regex that missed some spellings and left tenant_id declared twice, and an index prefix applied to an index that already led with tenant_id. Both failed loudly at migrate time, which is the good outcome. Tenant isolation is now proven on the write path for 147 tables, up from 32 at the start of this session. Gates 13/0, tests 5972 assertions 0 failures.

title: Recruitment, and the columns that were not in any migration either
detail: Building recruitment surfaced the second half of the same defect. Beyond creating whole tables inside controllers, SmartPRS 2 ALTERS them there too: an addCols() helper that adds a column if it is not present, called on every request. The candidate table `recruitment` is created with FOUR columns and grown to thirty-four by the page that lists it — so the offer itself (offered_ctc, offer_doj, offer_status, expected_ctc, skills, resume_url) is in no migration anywhere. A schema that depends on which pages have run cannot be reviewed, diffed or restored. Extracted 69 such columns across 20 tables and ported them, money arriving at the schema's own DECIMAL(18,4) rather than whatever precision it happened to have; the whole schema now reports one money type. Found one more thing while doing it: `overtime` is READ by PayrollGenController behind if (!Schema::hasTable('overtime')) return, and NOTHING in SmartPRS 2 creates it — so on an installation without that table, overtime is silently never paid. No error, no warning, a payslip that looks complete. Created it, with the columns that code reads. Recruitment then went in as five declared modules — job openings with the requisition workflow, candidates with a twelve-stage pipeline and the full offer, interviews by round with a recommendation, hiring drives, and onboarding — 445 form fields across 84 modules now. Two of my own mistakes, both caught by the spine rather than by me: the stub mapped Schema::table onto create so an ALTER tried to create an existing table, and company_id slipped through the column extractor without the rename because that extractor reads the addCols maps the earlier pass never saw. Gates 13/0, tests 5993 assertions 0 failures, 148 tables proving write-path isolation.

title: Customisation, and three checks of mine that were not checking
detail: This is the governing sentence of the rebuild given a form: change configuration, not code, by somebody who does not have a checkout. A customisation is stored as JSON against the tenant, versioned and append-only at the privilege level - the application account holds SELECT and INSERT on module_customisations and nothing else - and laid over config/modules.json at the single point every read passes through, Modules::all(). Applying it in fields() instead would have left the list showing the shipped columns while the form beneath it showed the customer's, which is the customisation-half-applied bug. What can be changed is a closed list and the refusals are the feature: table, key, permissions and lookup targets are structural, because an administrator renaming a field must not be able to repoint the screen at another table or take the permission off it, and a settings form that allows either is a privilege escalation with a nice label. Three of my own checks were not checking anything, and each is the same lesson again. First, the whole test file was vacuous: it used bare assert() and zend.assertions is -1 here, so I broke an assertion deliberately and the suite still passed - a check that silently checks nothing is worse than a missing one, and the only reason I know is that I tried to break it. Rewritten onto the harness's own ok(). Second, the required-and-hidden check read the override rather than the merged field, so a module that ships a field as required and is customised only to hide it passed the check and produced a screen that refuses every save for a box nobody can see. Third, no-change detection compared against what shipped rather than what is live, so resubmitting an unchanged form wrote another identical version and told the person it had saved. Also found and fixed: the local admin seeder wrote to the file store while the application reads MySQL, so it reported already seeded for an account that could not sign in - the same shape again, a check answering about the wrong thing. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6021 assertions 0 failures, 171 tables.

title: Letters, the money I wrote twice, and a tool that could only destroy
detail: An HR system's letters are the documents somebody keeps for twenty years and shows to a bank and to their next employer. SmartPRS 2 builds them in a controller per type; in practice most installations keep a Word file on a desktop, so the version that goes out depends on whose desktop. Seven templates now live in config/letters.json and one engine renders them. The rule the class exists for: a placeholder that resolves to nothing is a refusal, not a blank. An appointment letter that goes out reading 'your annual cost to company will be' is worse than one that failed to render, because it is signed, filed and acted on, and nobody reads six familiar paragraphs closely enough to see the gap - so the refusal names the fields, as HR would name them, and produces no text at all. A half-rendered draft is the thing that gets signed. An issued letter stores the text that went out rather than the template key, because re-rendering an experience certificate from today's wording years after it was signed is an overwritten record wearing a disguise. And a template's permissions are DERIVED from what it prints: a body using the money filter also requires employee.salary.view, because an offer letter and a warning letter are both a letter, and treating them as one permission is how somebody who may issue warnings ends up able to print everybody's CTC. Derived rather than declared, since a declaration that has to be remembered is forgotten on the eighth template. Two findings against myself. First, I wrote rupee formatting and rupees-in-words from scratch and only afterwards found Money::format() and Money::toWords() already in Platform, already on the Indian scale. My version grouped Western - 4,200,000 where an Indian salary reads 42,00,000 - and the second implementation is the one that drifts, on the line a salary dispute is settled by. Deleted mine. Second, the test that proved blanks are refused proved nothing: every field it removed was also in the template's requires list, so the requires check did all the work and the placeholder check was dead code that looked like a safeguard. Found by disabling the check and watching the suite pass; added the case for a placeholder nothing requires. Also, sorting issued letters newest-first cast non-numeric ids to zero, so the sort silently did nothing while looking sorted. Third, and larger: tools/db/migrate.php had no ledger, so the only way to apply a new migration was --fresh - dropping the database. That is not a tool limitation, it is a product that cannot be updated. There is now a migrations table, only pending files execute, and a database with tables but an empty ledger is REFUSED rather than assumed current, because a ledger claiming a schema is up to date while a column is missing is the same defect as every other check that checks nothing. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6075 assertions 0 failures, 171 tables.

title: The third bucket on a compliance screen
detail: Ejaz's business is debt collections, where a recovery agent whose DRA certificate has lapsed must not be allocated work and whose police clearance has expired must not go to a client site - these are findings against the bank as well as against the agency. So the compliance screen is not a nice-to-have here, and the way it usually fails is specific. Every compliance screen in every HR system reports two numbers, in date and expired. A row with no date recorded falls into neither, so it is silently counted as fine. An agency with two hundred agents and forty blank DRA expiry dates reads 160 in date, 0 expired, and believes it. The forty are what the audit finds. So NOT DETERMINED is a reported state here with its own count and its own list of names, never folded into compliant, and the summary line says it in words: 2 with no date recorded, which is not the same as in date. Four checks are declared in config/compliance.json with the table, the date column, the warning period, and - in words - what the lapse blocks, because a screen that reports a date without saying what the date prevents is a list nobody acts on. Findings name the person rather than the row id for the same reason. Three things that would have made it lie, all closed. A check whose table does not exist returns zero findings on the file store, which puts a clean line on the screen for a check that never looked at anything; it now refuses and says so. Worse, a check naming a column the table does not have would report EVERY row as no-date-recorded, which reads as two hundred people who never submitted a date and is in fact one wrong word in the declaration; that refuses too, naming the column. And MySQL's old 0000-00-00 read as a date is the year zero, which would report as two thousand years lapsed and bury every real finding - it is undetermined, not lapsed. The screen deliberately enforces nothing: refusing an allocation belongs at the point of the act, and a dashboard whose existence persuades people they are covered is worse than no dashboard. Verified live: one agent 18 days lapsed, one expiring in 28 days, two with no date at all, and pointing a check at a wrong column made the screen refuse by name. I also deleted an assertion of my own that compared 'Lapsed' with a ternary returning 'Lapsed' either way - vacuous, and the same mistake I keep finding. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6080 assertions 0 failures.

title: The promise three files kept making, and the inverted chain
detail: Three files in this codebase said some version of: a customer who wants one more approver above 50,000 rupees needs a release in SmartPRS 2, and here it is a threshold in config/workflows.json. That was true and it was not enough. A threshold in a JSON file on a server is a developer's edit. The promise was being kept for the person with a checkout and for nobody else, and I had written it down three times without noticing. Every approval chain now has a screen: the amount each step joins at, the SLA, whether a reason is demanded on approve or reject, and what the step is called. Stored as a version beside the module customisations - same table, same append-only privileges, key prefixed workflow: so the two cannot collide - and applied at Requests::workflows(), the single point every read passes through, so it changes the ROUTING and not only the page. A screen and a router disagreeing about who must approve is the worst possible place for a disagreement, and applying the overlay in chainFor() alone would have produced exactly that. What is NOT customisable is the control: which role decides a step, what the workflow is about, the permission needed to raise it, and whether a step is an approval at all. Raising a threshold is an administrator doing their job; changing who signs is an administrator removing the second person the approval exists for, through a settings form. The check that earns the file is the inverted chain. If finance sees claims over 5,000 and somebody sets the director to 1,000, then every claim between the two reaches the director and skips finance - the senior approver signs what the junior one never checked. Nothing errors. The routing does exactly what it was told and what it was told is backwards, which is why no test would catch it and no user would report it. It is refused, naming both steps and both figures, since which one is wrong is the customer's decision. I proved the defect is real rather than a rule I invented: configured that chain, routed a 2,000 rupee claim through it, and watched Finance come back skipped while Director applied. One bug of my own on the way: clearing a threshold back to empty unset the key from the change but merged the original step over it, so the old threshold came straight back - the cleared value silently did nothing, which is the exact failure mode this whole application is built against. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6098 assertions 0 failures.

title: The customer's own words, and the same lesson a third time
detail: Letter wording is now editable from inside the application, versioned per tenant in the same append-only table as the module and workflow customisations, and applied at the one point every read passes through - so the preview, the permission derivation and the text that gets issued are all the same letter. Three refusals at save time, and each one is a template that would otherwise fail on the day somebody actually needed the letter. A placeholder naming something an employment does not hold can never resolve, so the template would refuse for every person for ever; it is caught while it is one word in a box rather than six weeks later when HR cannot issue a relieving letter to somebody leaving today and the message names a field they have never heard of. A formatting filter that does not exist would print in the letter exactly as written, in a signed document. And the third is the same lesson this session keeps teaching me: a customer who rewrites only the body inherits the shipped required-fields list, so a new wording that stops printing the joining date leaves the template insisting on a field it no longer prints - and the change they typed says nothing about the required list, so a check reading the change would pass it. It only fires because the check reads the MERGED template. That is now three times in this session: the required-and-hidden field check on modules, the blank-placeholder check in letters that the requires list was quietly doing all the work for, and this. The pattern is always the same shape - the check reads what was typed rather than what will exist. There is a fourth safeguard against making the check itself vacuous: if the list of fields an employment holds comes back empty, the save is REFUSED rather than the placeholder check being skipped, because a check that runs against nothing passes everything. Verified live: an unknown placeholder, an unknown filter and a dropped required field each refused by name, then a genuinely rewritten offer letter saved and rendered - To KAVITA SHARMA, the post of Collections Executive at Hyderabad, joining on 01 October 2026, 42,00,000 rupees and the words to match. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6116 assertions 0 failures.

title: The fourth place to look, and the change that applies to nothing
detail: Three screens now let a customer change modules, approval chains and letter wording without a developer. That created a problem the code-first version did not have: the configuration is spread over three screens and a table, so nobody can answer what is different about our installation without looking in four places. There is now one place, and it lists every customised thing with its live version, how many versions are kept, who changed it and why. The finding it exists for is the orphan. A customisation stored against a key that is no longer declared anywhere - a module taken out of the registry, a template retired - sits in that table doing nothing, for ever, while whoever made the change believes it is in force. Nothing errors, nothing is missing from any screen, and the only symptom is that a change somebody remembers making is not there. It is the quietest way this table can fail, so orphans are named at the top of the screen rather than filtered out of the list, and they sort first. Proved it by planting one directly in the database: 1 customisation applies to nothing, retired-thing. The screen also says, in a table of its own, what CANNOT be changed and why - a module's table and permission, who decides a workflow step, a letter's key - and, more usefully, which declarations still have no screen at all. Reports and compliance checks are still file edits. Writing that down as a row that says not yet, rather than leaving the screen listing only the three that are done, is the same discipline as everywhere else here: a gap nobody names is a gap nobody closes, and a settings page that shows only what exists reads as complete. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6126 assertions 0 failures.

title: The report screen with no lock on it
detail: I went looking for the next thing to make customisable and found something worse. Reports.php has carried a line in its own docblock since the day I wrote it - a declaration file that composes SQL can reach any table by any path, and a report is exactly the feature somebody adds in a hurry - and the screen rendering those reports had no permission check on it at all. Not a weak one. None. Any signed-in user could open Annual CTC by department and read the total salary of every department in the company, from a table whose own module sits behind employee.view and whose salary field sits behind employee.salary.view. I wrote the warning and then built the thing it warns about, three screens later, and did not notice until I opened the file for an unrelated reason. The aggregate is what made it invisible to me: nobody thinks of a total as data. But a total by department with three people in it is three salaries, and a headcount by branch tells you where people are. A report now inherits the VIEW PERMISSION OF THE MODULE THAT DECLARES ITS TABLE, and a money report needs the salary permission on top. Derived from what the report reads, not written on the report, because a permission somebody has to remember to add to a new report is precisely the one they forget on the report they add in a hurry - which is the same reasoning as the letters, and the reason I could fix all sixteen at once instead of annotating them. A report over a table NO module declares is refused rather than shown: there is nothing to inherit from, and no rule found must never read as no rule applies. Reports that are not yours are listed and marked rather than hidden, because knowing a figure exists and that you may not see it is different from believing it does not exist - and the check runs on the URL as well as the list, since a report hidden from a menu but answerable by its address is a UI convention wearing a lock. Proved it by demoting my own account to viewer and asking for the salary report by URL: Denied, needs employee.view and employee.salary.view. The test asserts it for every shipped report rather than the two I looked at, and I broke the money clause deliberately to check the test was really testing - five failures. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6154 assertions 0 failures.

title: The dashboard I had just built a hole into
detail: Rebuilt the dashboard in SmartPRS 2's shape - the five-tile KPI strip, the panel grid, the progress bars - using SmartPRS 2's own stylesheet. What is different underneath is that it runs no queries. Every figure names a report and the report is the only thing that counts anything, because SmartPRS 2's dashboard has its own SQL in DashboardController and its employee list has more, so the headcount on the dashboard and the headcount on the report screen are two answers to one question computed by two pieces of code with two sets of filters. When they eventually disagree the argument cannot be settled, since neither number can be traced. Which tiles exist, which report feeds each, and whether a tile takes the report's total or one of its rows is config/dashboard.json. Two rules earned their place, and one of them is a hole I had opened myself an hour earlier. I had just put the total-CTC report behind the salary permission after finding the reports screen unguarded. A dashboard tile showing that same total to anybody who can open the landing page hands it straight back, and it is the easiest leak in any HR system to miss because nobody thinks of a summary as data. So a tile fed by a report the viewer cannot open carries NO value at all - not a value the template is trusted to hide - and shows a padlock. Verified by demoting my own account to viewer: five padlocks, and the string 42,00,000 appears nowhere in the page. The second rule: a tile whose report does not exist shows a dash and a reason, never a zero. A KPI reading 0 because somebody renamed a report is indistinguishable from a real zero, and a real zero on a dashboard is acted on - nobody has taken leave this month, nothing is pending, everything is settled. A bucket the report genuinely never produced IS zero, and says which kind of zero it is so the reader does not have to guess. Probed both by breaking them: ignoring report permissions cost seven failures, showing a missing report as zero cost two. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6233 assertions 0 failures.

title: Three locks, each inside the last
detail: The list screens are SmartPRS 2's now - page header, stat tiles, filter bar, avatar cells, status badges, rupees in mono - and all 84 modules got them from one edit, because there is one module screen rather than eighty-four index views. That is the architecture argument made visible: in SmartPRS 2 the avatar tint array, the badge map and the rupee formatting are copied into employees/index and payslips/index and loans/index, so a status colour that is wrong is wrong on one screen and right on the others. Here it is derived from the column names once - anything called status or state or stage becomes a badge, anything that reads as money is formatted as rupees - and a module that wants something different says so. Derived rather than declared because eighty-four modules will not each get a hand-written presentation block, and a scheme that needs one stays unapplied on the sixty nobody got to. Then three locks, each found inside the last, and each the same mistake at a smaller scale. First: the stat tile above the employee list totals CTC, which is exactly the figure I had put behind the salary permission on the reports screen two increments earlier. Locked it. Then I read the rendered page for a viewer and the tile said not yours to see while the table beside it said 42,00,000 in every row - so I had locked the report, locked the dashboard tile, locked the stat tile, and left the column printed. A field can now carry its own permission: not rendered, not offered on the form, and NOT WRITABLE, because a field hidden from a template but accepted by the save is a lock on the door of a room with no wall. It defaults to DENY when nobody is there to ask, since a field-level lock that defaults to open is open everywhere it was not explicitly wired. Third, and the worst: making the save refuse to write ctc ERASED it. The file store replaced the whole document on a partial write while SqlStore issues UPDATE SET for the columns it was given, so the same save updated a name on MySQL and blanked every unsent column on files. A viewer editing somebody's name would have silently deleted their salary. A lock that deletes the thing it is protecting is worse than no lock. The two stores now agree, and a probe that restores the old behaviour costs three failures. One more note on method: the not-writable assertion passed on its first run for the wrong reason - both saves were failing on a missing required field, so nothing was written either way and the test proved nothing. The paired assertion that the permitted save must SUCCEED is what caught it. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6260 assertions 0 failures.

title: A warning that had quietly stopped being able to appear
detail: The sign-in page is SmartPRS 2's: the navy panel with the brand and three feature rows, the white form panel, the gradient button, its own stylesheet. Building it put the two standing warnings at the top of that page and I noticed only one of them was there. The default-credential banner looked for is_local_default on the user row. The ported users table has twelve columns and that is not one of them - so on MySQL the flag could never be true, the banner could never appear, and the text it would have shown says it has no dismiss button and disappears only when the account does. It had disappeared while the account was still there. I made it worse myself: when I fixed the seeder to write to the same store the application reads, I dropped the is_local_default key from the insert, because the column does not exist and MySQL would have refused the write. That was the right fix to the seeder and it silently removed the last thing that could set the flag - on the file store, where it had still been working. So the check now tests the CONDITION rather than a flag: the account's own address, named once in Session::LOCAL_DEFAULT_EMAIL and shared by the seeder and the banner. An email cannot silently stop existing. The test seeds a user row exactly as the ported schema stores one, with no flag anywhere, and asserts the warning still finds it; putting the old flag-based check back costs a failure. Separately, the lowered password floor is now its own notice rather than a sentence inside the account warning. Deleting the seeded account would have taken the floor warning away with it and left the floor at 8 - one condition hidden behind another is a check that stops checking for a reason nobody wrote down. Both now fire independently, and both are on the sign-in page, which is where a default credential is worth saying. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6266 assertions 0 failures.

title: Twenty-nine reads of a column that does not exist
detail: I went to fix the attendance screen, which said Choose an employment from the Employments list and gave no way to choose one - a dead end that makes somebody navigate away, find a row and come back to start the task the screen exists for. It has a picker now. What the fix uncovered is the real entry. This application had been reading employee_code from the employees table. The ported table calls it emp_code. Twenty-nine reads in the front controller plus one each in the payroll register and full-and-final, every one of them asking for a column that has never existed on the real schema - and every one of them working, for months, because the file store returns whatever key it was handed and the fixtures I wrote used the same wrong name. A name that is wrong consistently looks right. It would have surfaced the first time somebody ran a payroll register against a real month, with a blank code column on every line. The write path was worse than the reads. The Employments create form wrote employee_code, gross, joined_on, bank_account and bank_ifsc - five columns, none of them on the table, which are emp_code, ctc, doj, bank_acc and ifsc. That form could never have added an employment to a real database. MySQL refused all five, loudly and by name, which is the store doing its job; the point is that nothing had ever asked it. There is now one place that answers what an employment's code is - emp_code first because that is what the table has, employee_code after because older rows and fixtures still carry it and silently dropping them would turn a naming defect into missing data, and a stated absence rather than an empty string when there is neither, because a payslip with a blank code is one nobody can match to a person. The test asserts against the SCHEMA THE MIGRATIONS BUILD rather than against a fixture, so it cannot agree with the same mistake twice: it reads the blueprint, checks the column this code uses is one the migrations create, and separately checks the old name is NOT on the table, since if both existed neither would be authoritative. It also asserts the five columns the create form used to write are absent and the six it writes now are present. Putting the wrong name back costs five failures. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6290 assertions 0 failures.

title: The check I wrote to find the bug, which could not find the bug
detail: Fixing the attendance dead end turned up employee_code against a table whose column is emp_code, and the obvious question was how many more there were. So I wrote tools/smoke.php: start the server, sign in, open every route, fail on any PHP warning. It found gross and joined_on immediately. Then it reported PASS. It was lying. PHP's built-in server has html_errors on, so the body carries Fatal error in bold tags and my check was matching the literal string Fatal error colon - which never appears. The employees screen had been dying inside a table cell on every single request while my brand-new check, written specifically to catch pages that are wrong, printed clean. Within the hour. The fix is not a better string match, because that is the same bet again. A page that dies stops rendering, so it never reaches its closing tag: the check now requires the document to be complete, and separately reads the server's own error log, which gets the message whatever display_errors and html_errors are set to. A truncated page cannot lie about being truncated. Two more things it could not see, both found by other means. It only visited routes bare, and most screens render an empty branch with no row in front of them - which touches none of the code that reads a row's columns, which is where every one of these defects lives. It now visits each route twice, with a real employment id, and that found leave and payroll immediately. And it cannot see WRITES at all, because a refused write leaves the page rendering happily. There is now a test that drives every put() through a recording store and holds the keys against the blueprint the migrations build, which found five more tables writing names that do not exist - attendance_logs, attendance_corrections, payroll_runs, payroll_corrections, settlements - plus a screen reading a table called leave_requests that has never existed in any schema, so every leave decision was recorded in the audit trail as a change from nothing. The leaves table alone had six wrong names, and only the first produced a warning: the others were hidden behind it because the filter never matched, so nothing downstream ever read a row. Renaming the one would have silenced the warning and left the leave screen showing zero requests for ever. Proven end to end now, against MySQL: a request submitted, approved, and a ledger debit that names it. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6560 assertions 0 failures, smoke 48 visits 0 complaining.

title: Eleven screens, three agents, and two bugs found by looking
detail: The remaining hand-built screens are in SmartPRS 2's anatomy now: page header with a real subtitle and a primary action, stat tiles where there were already figures, card headers, the badge vocabulary for states, and money through Money::format() so it groups on the Indian scale. Employments, leave, payroll, register, structure, employee view, inbox, approvals, audit trail, full-and-final and attendance. The rules that mattered were the ones about what NOT to do: presentation only, no condition or permission check or refusal message or calculation touched, and nothing hidden behind the explanation fold. That last one is a rule because I broke it myself two increments ago and folded a permission denial out of sight. So the payroll register still says Not approved in full width, in red, above the fold, and the compliance screen still leads with what it could not determine. Two real bugs turned up not from a test but from looking at the screenshots. The default-credential banner had an unclosed span and a stray closing div, so the browser was closing the content div early on every page in the application; because content is flex:1 it then stretched to fill the viewport and pushed the page header down by 250 pixels on any short screen. Every automated check passed throughout - the markup was invalid, not the logic - and it was visible the moment somebody looked at the structure screen. The other: an em-dash entity passed through the escaper, so the salary structure printed the literal characters ampersand m d a s h semicolon in its Rate column for every component with no flat amount. Both are the kind of thing that has no test and needs an eye. Three agents ran in parallel for this stretch, on disjoint files: one proving the smoke check was non-vacuous, one seeding representative data so the smoke had rows to render, one porting the write paths. The seeding agent is the reason the rest worked - it reported that the smoke check's coverage is only as good as the rows present, which was true and was the gap that let the employees screen fatal unnoticed. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6560 assertions 0 failures, smoke 48 visits 0 complaining.

title: A parser that forgives cannot find something unforgivable
detail: Two things this round. An agent closed the last two customisation gaps - the Configuration screen had a table admitting that reports and compliance checks were still file edits, and that row is now false and removed. A report's label, question, group and filters are editable; its table and its money flag are not, because permissionsFor() derives the permission in front of the figure from exactly those two, so a form that could set them would be a privilege escalation with a settings screen in front of it. A check's label, warning period and blocks sentence are editable; its table and date column are not, because a check pointed at another column reports every row as no date recorded, which reads as two hundred people who never submitted a date and is one wrong word. The refusal that earns the reports work is the filter on a column the table does not have: the report comes back empty, and an empty report is indistinguishable from there is nothing to report - somebody reads 0 agents on notice off a screen and believes it. The second thing is about my own checking. The unclosed span that was closing the content div on every page in the application was found by a person looking at a screenshot, while the test suite, the gates and the smoke check all passed. So I added markup validation to the smoke check, reached for DOMDocument, and it reported NOTHING for that exact input. libxml's HTML parser silently repairs bad nesting - which is precisely what a browser does, and precisely why the defect was invisible in the first place. A parser that forgives cannot be used to find something unforgivable. So the check counts instead: opening tags against closing tags, for the thirteen elements this codebase always closes explicitly, forgiving nothing. And then the probe. I reintroduced the defect and the check still passed - which for a moment looked like the second vacuous check in a row, and was worse than that: my probe string no longer existed in the file, because the restyle had rewritten that region, so I had never reintroduced anything. The probe was measuring nothing and reporting reassurance. Probed against the real markup it fails on all 52 visits, because that banner is on every page. Two lessons stacked: check the check, and then check that the way you broke it actually broke it. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6641 assertions 0 failures, smoke 52 visits 0 complaining.

title: The payslip that shows its working
detail: Every payroll product produces a payslip and this one did not. It does now, and the rules around it are stricter than around a screen, because a payslip is the one thing this system makes that leaves the building - it goes to a bank for a loan, to a landlord, to the next employer, and to a tribunal when something has gone wrong. It is READ from the closed run and never recomputed. The register already refuses to recompute a closed month; a payslip that recomputed would be worse, because it would do so months later against a structure that has since changed, and the employee's copy and the company's copy would then differ with nobody able to say which was the one issued. Every line carries the sentence the run itself wrote when it computed that figure - 50% of 96,000 equals 48,000; the balance of 96,000 after 67,200 of other earnings, computed by subtraction so the lines sum to the gross by construction rather than to within a paisa of it; D-PT is a flat 200 and does NOT prorate, because a flat statutory amount is for the month and prorating it would under-deduct against a return that expects it whole. SmartPRS 2's payslip prints amounts. This one prints the arithmetic, because the question an employee actually asks is never what the HRA is, it is why it changed. Not regenerated at print time either: a fresh explanation of an old number is a guess about what the rules used to be. Three refusals. An unapproved run produces a payslip marked draft on its face - withholding it would be wrong because HR has to check the draft, but an employee must never be handed one that looks final and is not. A month with no closed payroll produces nothing, because a blank document with somebody's name on it looks like a month in which they earned nothing. And an employment not in the run is a different fact from paid nothing this month, only one of which is somebody's mistake - so the month dropdown offers only the months that employment is actually IN. On shape: the payslip takes the RUN, not the register that found it. Handing it the register would give it the ability to recompute, which is the one thing it must not do, and it also means the whole thing tests against an array with no database, structure, attendance engine or leave policy standing behind it. That was not the first design - the first took the register, and the test needed a stub, and needing a stub was the tell. Also this round: an agent built php tools/check.php, one command for tests, gates, phpstan, deptrac and smoke, with SKIPPED as a first-class state that is never folded into PASS. Its exit policy is right - a skip is loud but not fatal, EXCEPT when smoke could not run on a full run, because smoke refusing to run is precisely the failure mode this codebase is disciplined against. You may decline to run a check; you may not fail to notice that it did not run. And it found a stale hand-written route list in the navigation test, which failed for the wrong reason the moment the payslip route was added - now read from the front controller like the smoke check does. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6666 assertions 0 failures, smoke 54 visits 0 complaining.

title: The rule the code meant and the rule the database enforced
detail: Two things, and the second was found by accident while proving the first. There was no CSRF protection in this application. None - grep for csrf across every file returned zero. Every POST was cross-site forgeable, including the ones that approve a salary increment, close a payroll month, publish a salary structure and change a customer's approval thresholds. It is one token per session, compared with hash_equals, and ONE check above every action rather than a list of actions that are checked. That shape matters: an opt-in list is the thing that gets forgotten on the eighth form, and the rule here is derived instead - if there is a session identity to abuse, the POST must prove it came from a page this session was shown. Twenty-four forms, all carrying it, every one exercised with a token, without one, and with a token from a different session. Sign-in and first-run enrolment are the two that cannot carry one, and both are commented in place with why they are safe rather than left silently unchecked. Then the accident. The agent added a second employee to test a form and the page 500ed. Leave::credit() treats an entry as already posted when the EMPLOYMENT and the reference both match, which is the right rule. The unique index on leave_entries is tenant_id plus source_reference, with no employment in it. Two different rules for the same thing, and the database's was the narrower one. So the references read opening:CL and accrual:CL:2026-01 - naming the leave type and the month but not the person. The in-memory check passed for the second employee, because it compares the employment; the INSERT then collided with the FIRST employee's row, because the index does not. The employee row had already landed by then, so it left somebody on the books with no opening leave balance and a fatal on the screen. This application could hold exactly one employee. Invisible on the file store, which has no unique index at all - the same family as every other defect this rebuild has found, and found the same way: by doing something real against a real schema. The reference now carries the employment, which makes the tenant-wide index mean what the code means, and a test asserts every reference this class writes contains it so the next reference format somebody invents cannot quietly drop it. The dedupe also matches the OLD reference form, so re-running an accrual over a ledger that already exists does not double every opening balance a customer has. Proven end to end: two employees added through the real form, both landing, each with their own opening balances and accruals. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6864 assertions 0 failures, smoke 54 visits 0 complaining.

title: The column that had been there all along
detail: users.employee_id has been in this schema since the day it was ported. Nothing has ever read it. SubjectContext's own docblock says actorEmployeeId is users.employee_id; DataScope has thirteen scope types with covers() and a SQL predicate(); Persistence\Repository compiles the self scope to employee_id = :scope_employee. All of it written, all of it tested, none of it called - and the surface handed both roles DataScope::tenantWide() and asked no further question. So every screen in this product answered which records with all of them in this tenant, including the one titled what an employee sees, which rendered anybody's payslip and complete leave ledger to anybody who changed a sequential integer in the address bar. The platform was ahead of the surface, and the gap was a security boundary. The session now carries the employment binding and one Scope class asks DataScope whether a row is yours. It asks rather than comparing two strings, and the comment says why: the comparison would be right today and would know nothing about direct reports or a reporting tree the moment either is granted, and a second implementation of an authorisation rule is always the one that gets it wrong. An unbound account sees nothing of its own rather than everything - DataScope's self already resolves an unbound actor to the EMPTY set, which is the safe direction to be wrong in. The two refusals are deliberately different: that is somebody else's record is a person looking at a colleague, and this account is not linked to an employment is an administrator's configuration problem wearing the costume of a permission error. Collapsing them sends somebody to the wrong person for help. Proven live: a viewer linked to SP-001 opens ?r=me with no id and gets their own payslip, and gets refused on a colleague's. Separately, the exposure sweep an agent built - which reads the real secret values out of the database and asserts they do not appear on a page served to somebody who may not see them - reported five of its seven value classes as NOT ASSERTED, because the demo data had no bank accounts, IFSC codes, PAN, UAN or Aadhaar in it. Honest, and blind. A check that cannot see is the thing this product is written against, and the fix was the data rather than the check: it now hunts 117 values instead of 57, and unlocking PAN on one module makes it fire by name. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6882 assertions 0 failures, smoke 54 visits, exposure 71 visits 0 exposing.

title: The refusal that was worth nothing with the directory above it
detail: The scope mechanism existed after the last increment but only one screen used it. An agent built the sweep that proves the rest: sign in as a viewer bound to one employment, request every route pointed at a colleague, assert their name, emp_code, email and mobile are absent from the page - and, crucially, assert the viewer can still see their OWN record, because a sweep where nothing is reachable is measuring a broken application rather than a secure one. It found thirteen. Three were what I expected: leave, attendance and letters read an id out of the query string and fetched whoever it named. The other ten were the interesting ones, and the tool distinguished them by BEHAVIOUR rather than by prose - it noticed the leak was identical whether the parameter pointed at a colleague or at nobody, which means the parameter was not what was leaking. They were pickers. The payslip screen, the letters screen, the attendance screen and the employments list each enumerated every employment in the tenant, name and code, in a dropdown above a screen that would have refused a colleague's row. A refusal is worth nothing with the directory printed above it. That is a distinction I would not have drawn from reading the code, and a value-grep would not have drawn either: it took a tool that fetched the same route two ways and compared. Two mistakes of my own while fixing them. I put an HTML comment inside a PHP block and the file stopped parsing - caught immediately by php -l, which is the cheap check doing its job. And I reached for a permission called attendance.punch.view.other that does not exist in the catalogue. An uncatalogued permission FAILS CLOSED here, so it would have padlocked the column for everybody including the administrator and read as a bug rather than as a rule; I checked all five names against the catalogue before committing rather than trusting that they sounded right. Thirteen to zero, control still firing on four screens, and the sweep is a slot in check.php that a silent skip fails the build on - the same treatment as smoke and exposure, for the same reason. Gates 13 checks 0 violations, tests 6882 assertions 0 failures, smoke 54 visits, exposure 71 visits 117 values, scope 216 visits 0 leaking.

title: A guard that refuses everybody refuses the attacker too
detail: The scope sweep passed clean and had a hole in it that it reported honestly and could not close: signed in as a viewer, five routes were permission refusals, so it learned nothing about whose rows they would show. NOT CHECKED, said so, and stopped. So the sweep now takes a role - php tools/scope.php --role=administrator --tenant-wide - and INVERTS its assertion: an administrator holds payroll.view, which means any employment's pay, so the colleague appearing is the permission working and reporting it as a leak would be the tool failing the product for obeying its own grants. What is asserted instead is that the routes are reachable and show both records, because a screen that shows nobody is exactly how the viewer sweep's 'no colleague here' becomes a clean result over nothing. It failed on the first run. Three routes - attendance, leave, letters - were BLIND: the administrator could not see a colleague either.
