The row guards I added last increment name employee.list, employee.document.view, leave.balance.view_others and attendance.day.view.history, and every one of those names was checked against the permission catalogue when the guards went in. They are all in the catalogue. They were granted to NO ROLE AT ALL. So every guard fell to its self-only branch for every account in the product: an HR administrator could not open a colleague's leave. Existing in the catalogue is not the same as being held by somebody, and the check I ran last time only proved the first. No security sweep could have found it, because a guard that refuses everybody refuses the attacker too and reads as a pass in every direction that was being measured. It took a probe signed in as somebody who SHOULD see the colleague. Then the two ungated screens: ?r=trail had no permission on it - the audit trail is every act in the tenant with actor and payload, a salary change reads back off it in full, and it sat behind the narrowest door there is, being signed in. Now audit.tenant.read. And ?r=requests printed requester, note and amount for every request in the organisation, one click above ?r=request&id= which correctly derived its permission from the module the request is about. A row-level gate under a list rendering the same rows is not a gate. Narrowed rather than denied, so a person always sees what they raised themselves, with the withheld count stated rather than the list quietly shortening itself. Chasing that one found the real defect underneath: the increments module declares view: employee.view, which a viewer holds, and puts employee.salary.view on new_ctc - so the module screen masked the amount correctly while the increment REQUEST printed the same number on its face and inherited only the module's weaker view permission. The field guard was bypassed by rendering the value somewhere the field did not exist. permissionFor() now inherits the permission on the field the amount comes from when the workflow names one. Masking a column on one screen and printing it on another is not a permission system, it is a habit.

title: The role in the middle is where a scope goes wrong
detail: Three things, two of them found by the checks rather than by me. A manager role now exists, which is what DataScope's direct_reports was waiting for - ten permissions, every one verified in the catalogue, no payroll and no salary, because 'who reports to me' and 'what they are paid' are different questions and a manager needing the second is a decision somebody makes deliberately. Then payroll reversal, which closes an inconsistency that had been sitting in plain sight: Payslip.php reads run.status === 'approved' and watermarks anything else as not authorised, Register.php's own header said 'no approval step, no bank file, no reversal', and nothing in the product ever set those fields - so every payslip the system could produce was watermarked unauthorised, forever. Reversal records the opposite of a month rather than editing it, so both the payment and the withdrawal are on file and 'what did we actually pay in March' keeps its answer. It is gated on payroll.run.approve, not payroll.run: withdrawing a signature is the signature's own authority. Now the two the checks found. Declaring the manager role silently handed a manager the entire tenant. Scope::covers() short-circuited on a mayReadOthers boolean, and employee.list, leave.balance.view_others and attendance.day.view.history are held by BOTH the administrator and the manager - so the row guard stopped running for the exact account it was introduced for. A sweep signed in as a manager found nine of them, against demo data with no reporting lines, where the right answer everywhere was 'yourself'. The permission decides WHETHER an account reads beyond itself; the scope decides HOW FAR. Fixing that broke the administrator instead: app.php was deciding who had a team by asking a permission - may they decide leave - and the administrator holds that too, so it was narrowed to its own team and went blind on attendance, leave and letters. Caught by the tenant-wide sweep within a minute. A permission says what a role may do; only the role declaration says how much of the organisation is theirs, so reach() now says it out loud in Authorisation next to the grants. And the sweep itself had a landmine in it: once the demo data grew reporting lines it could pick a colleague who was actually a direct report, which a manager may correctly read, and report the scope working as a leak - flaky depending on which two rows were richest that day. It now picks somebody who does not report to the probe, and refuses outright if nobody qualifies rather than measuring the wrong thing.

title: A role nobody can assign is a role nobody has
detail: The manager role was declared, scoped to direct reports, unit-tested and swept by three security runs - and completely unreachable, because the only way to make somebody a manager was editing users.status in MySQL by hand. There was no way to create an account at all; the seeded local administrator was the entire population. So: an accounts screen, and the interesting part of it is the refusals rather than the forms. An account cannot change its own role, in either direction - upwards is granting yourself a permission nobody gave you, downwards locks you out and the person who could fix it is the person who just broke it. The last administrator cannot be demoted, because a tenant with no administrator cannot be administered and there is no support desk in this product to undo it from outside. An employment already linked to another account is refused: two accounts claiming to be the same person makes 'whose row is this' unanswerable, which is the exact question Scope exists to answer. An undeclared role is refused with the reason spelled out - an undeclared role is not a SMALLER role, the decider grants it nothing, so the account would be created and be silently unable to do anything. And unlinking states its consequence rather than just doing it: the account then sees nothing of its own, not everything. The screen is gated on access.user.list/create/update rather than tenant.settings.update, which the administrator already held and which would have been one word shorter to write - but changing the company's address and deciding who may sign in are not the same power, and the day they need separating is the day somebody discovers they were the same permission all along. Two other things worth writing down. The role and the employment are presented as two separate questions on purpose: the role decides what a person may do, the employment decides whose rows they see, and collapsing them is the classic HR-system mistake - a manager and an administrator both open the leave screen and only one should see the whole company on it. And the test suite reported 4564 assertions where it had reported 6965, which looked like a catastrophe and was MySQL having stopped: the database-backed files skip rather than fail, so the suite stayed green while examining two thirds of what it thought it did. The skip is reported per file, which is the only reason it was visible at all - a silent skip there would have been a green suite over nothing.

title: A wrong number with correct working under it
detail: An audit of the whole repo against the twenty-five specification parts found the defect this project existed to avoid, and it had been sitting in the middle of the product the entire time. employees.ctc holds a YEAR's cost - 7,20,000 - and the payroll register handed that figure to the run as THE MONTH's GROSS. Every payslip the product could produce was twelve times too high. Seven thousand assertions passed over it: the money arithmetic was exact, the components summed, the fingerprint verified, the reconciliation balanced, the net was gross minus deductions to the paisa. Every one of those compared the system against ITSELF. And under each line the payslip printed its working - '50% of 7,20,000 = 3,60,000' - which is arithmetically true, so a person reading it sees the sum check out and concludes the input must be right. A wrong number with correct working under it is worse than a wrong number alone, because the working is what persuades somebody to trust it. The fix is a declared, effective-dated contracted_cost_basis on the salary structure rather than a /12 in the register, because whether a customer quotes annual or monthly CTC is their fact and not ours, and a basis this build does not recognise is REFUSED rather than defaulted - 'yearly' silently meaning monthly would reintroduce the same twelve-times error through the spelling of a config value. The new test asserts rupee figures a person can check by hand, which is the only kind of assertion that could have caught this: a test saying 'the parts sum to the whole' is satisfied by a whole twelve times too big. Second finding, the same shape: four gates enforcing the seven laws - no-float-money, no-empty-catch, no-pii-in-logs, strict-types - were rooted at src/ and reported PASS over fourteen thousand lines of surface/ and public/, the only code a user's request ever reaches. Pointing them at those directories produced about fifty violations immediately, and surface/ really did decide which approver an expense claim needs by comparing floats. All of them are now fixed or declared: the eight that remain are bar widths and count formatting, each one keyed by file and line in tools/gates/allow/floats.php with a reason - an allow file the check's own docblock had promised for the life of the project and never read, so an entry in it was inert. Third, the owner asked to connect the project to a database the way SmartPRS 2 does. His standing instruction is that SmartPRS 2 is never edited, and the tempting reading - point SmartPRS 3's .env at the smartprs database - would have had the next migration run alter the system his business runs on today. So the importer copies out and refuses to run at all if the two databases are the same name, and the source is reached through a wrapper with one method that refuses any statement that is not a SELECT, with the MySQL session set read-only as well. Testing it against a stand-in database found a real defect on the first run - the ported tables carry NOT NULL timestamps with no default - which is now filled with the import time and nothing else: any OTHER mandatory column the source lacks is refused rather than invented, because a made-up value in a column somebody made mandatory is a lie the database was specifically asked to prevent.

title: A created account is not a working account
detail: The banner did its job and told him the product was running on JSON files with the reason on it: SQLSTATE 1524, plugin mysql_native_password not loaded. MySQL 8.4 REMOVED that plugin, and a Laragon my.ini that still names it as the default authentication plugin makes every account created with a bare IDENTIFIED BY unusable - while CREATE USER reports success, mysql prints nothing, and the setup script moves on to the next step. Three failures in a row that each reported success. The grant script now ASKS the server which authentication plugins are ACTIVE and names one explicitly, preferring caching_sha2_password, and refuses with the list it found if the server has neither rather than falling back to a default it cannot name. Then the deeper problem, which is not about MySQL: nothing in setup ever tried the account it had just created. So a new tools/db/verify-connection.php runs as step 2b, connects as the application account, and stops the setup there - next to the step that caused it - instead of letting the person discover it in a banner three steps later. Its first version was itself the mistake it exists to prevent: the write probe created a TEMPORARY table, which needs a privilege the least-privilege grant script deliberately withholds, so it reported FAIL against a correctly configured install. A check that fails on a healthy system is worse than no check, because it teaches whoever runs setup that the red line is normal. It reads SHOW GRANTS instead. And the 1044 branch says two things rather than one: from an account granted table by table on one database, 'this database does not exist' and 'you hold nothing on it' are the same refusal, and a setup message that confidently names the wrong cause sends somebody to fix something that was not broken.

title: The setup script had no first step
detail: He ran the setup script and got 'M' is not recognized as an internal or external command, followed by the DB_USERNAME refusal. Two separate faults, both mine. The batch file was written with Unix line endings and em dashes - cmd.exe misparsed it and reported an error naming a letter, which points at nothing that is actually wrong and sends somebody looking in the wrong place entirely. It is CRLF and ASCII now, with a comment saying why so nobody helpfully reformats it. The second was worse because it was honest and still useless: DB_USERNAME is blank on purpose - Law 2 gives the application an account with no ALTER/CREATE/DROP and migrations a separate privileged one, so there are two accounts to make - and every tool that could have made them needed one of them to already exist. migrate.php wanted the migrator; grant-application-account.php connects AS the migrator to grant to the app. The first run had no way in, and the refusal told the person to invent two accounts and two passwords by hand, which is how a local password ends up being 'root' on a laptop that later gets demoed from. tools/db/bootstrap-local.php is that missing first step: it creates both accounts with generated 40-character passwords that are never printed, writes them into .env line by line so every comment survives, keeps the old file as .env.bak, and refuses outright unless APP_ENV=local, because a tool that can edit a server's .env eventually edits a production one at eleven at night. Building it found four things that only running it could find. MariaDB rejects IDENTIFIED WITH <plugin> BY, which is exactly the syntax MySQL 8.4 needs - so the plugin choice now lives in one helper that asks the server what it is before deciding whether to name a plugin at all. The migrator could not create the application account, because that needs the global CREATE USER privilege it correctly does not hold; the grant script now only GRANTs, and the migrator gets WITH GRANT OPTION scoped to its one database rather than the global power to make accounts. Checking whether the account exists first needed to read mysql.user, which is a privilege this connection should not have either - a check that needs more rights than the thing it is checking is the same mistake one level up, so the GRANT is attempted and the server's answer is reported. And FLUSH PRIVILEGES on the last line needed the global RELOAD privilege and does nothing after a GRANT anyway: a habit copied from scripts that edit mysql.user by hand, turning a completed run into a failed one on its final statement.

title: The parser that blamed the file
detail: Every failure in his run traced to one line: I used parse_ini_file() to read .env in three new tools. PHP's INI parser comments with a semicolon, not a hash - and his .env, like every .env, comments with a hash, and one of those comments reads '# Instants are stored UTC (spine S16).' So parse_ini_file does not skip the comment or return a partial array. It raises a syntax error and returns FALSE, and every value the caller wanted is simply gone. What made it hard to see is that nothing reported a parsing problem. bootstrap-local.php announced 'APP_ENV is "", not "local"' about a file whose second line says APP_ENV=local and refused to run; migrate.php lost DB_DATABASE and went looking in a database nobody named. Both blamed his file, and his file was correct. The reader that handles this project's .env has existed the whole time - Surface\Database::env(), which the grant script already used - and I re-derived it three times in one sitting, wrongly each time. That is the failure this codebase punishes more than any other, so it is now structural rather than remembered: tests/one_env_reader_test.php asserts that nothing anywhere calls parse_ini_file, and asserts as its own non-vacuity check that parse_ini_file really does return FALSE on this exact file shape - if PHP handled it, the rule would be pedantry rather than a defect. The guard's first version scanned text and failed on three COMMENTS, each one a note explaining why parse_ini_file is not used; a check that fails on the documentation of its own rule is one somebody deletes, so it reads tokens. Probed by reintroducing a real call: one failure, removed, green.

title: Already configured, and not working
detail: The setup script printed 'Already configured. Skipping.' and then failed two lines later with the plugin error it exists to fix. The reason is the same sentence I had already written into verify-connection.php and then failed to apply one step earlier: A NAME IN A CONFIGURATION FILE IS NOT A WORKING ACCOUNT. Step 1 decided whether to create the database accounts by running findstr over .env - if DB_USERNAME had a value, it skipped. On his machine the accounts had been created by an earlier run with an authentication plugin MySQL 8.4 no longer loads, so .env was complete and correct and the accounts behind it could not sign in. The step that would have repaired them skipped, on the strength of the file. It now asks the SERVER: bootstrap-local.php --if-broken opens a connection as each of the two accounts and only skips when both actually sign in. Tested in both directions, which for this check is the whole point - break the app account on the server while leaving .env untouched, and it detects and recreates; leave everything healthy, and it skips. And migrate.php printed 'Start MySQL/MariaDB (in Laragon: Start All)' for every connection failure including this one, so it told somebody to start a service that was already running, three lines after a step that had just talked to it. A message that names the wrong cause costs more than no message, because it is followed. It now answers 1524 and 1045 with what each of them actually means.

title: Four things that were not true
detail: The audit's worst section was not the missing features, it was the four places where the product said something it did not do. All four are closed, and none of them needed a compliance owner - the fix for claiming what is not true is to stop claiming it. First, the payslip. PayslipCalculator printed 'a flat statutory amount' as the derivation of EVERY flat component, whatever it was, and the shipped structure has one: a 200 rupee deduction with no state, no slab and no legal basis, which arrived on the employee's document described as statutory. The engine cannot know whether a flat figure answers to a statute - only a signed pack from a compliance owner knows that, and this build has none - so it now states what it actually did: a flat amount declared in the salary structure, not derived from a rate or a slab. Second, the appointment letter tells a new joiner that provident fund will be deducted in accordance with the law. That sentence is a normal clause and is not the thing to change; the defect was that the product prints it and computes no PF, and nobody was told. Letters::promisesNotKept() now derives the mismatch from the letter's own text against the structure's declared flags, following the pattern permissionsFor() already set, and the letters screen reports it above the preview as a warning rather than a gate - the letter is legitimate, the silence was the defect. Deliberately, a wage-base flag does NOT count as coverage: pf_base on an earning assembles a base and remits nothing, and treating it as coverage would have cleared the exact letter the audit found. Third, config/workflows.json claimed in its own note that Platform\Workflow ran the chains and that no workflow-specific code existed anywhere. Both false: Surface\Requests is 384 lines of it, and the engine is unwired. A configuration file that misdescribes its own engine is worse than one with no note, because it is read by the person deciding whether a customer's requirement is a config change or a release. Fourth, sla_hours is editable on the configure screen, ten steps declare one, and nothing reads it - set 48 hours and at hour 49 nothing happens. The screen now says so where the field is, because somebody typing a number into a field is entitled to assume it does something, and an SLA that exists only as a number is worse than no SLA: it is the one people believe they have. A footnote worth keeping: my edits shifted line numbers and the file:line entries in the float allow-list stopped matching, so the gate spoke up about six lines it had been told to ignore. That is the self-cleaning behaviour those keys were chosen for, working the first time it was tested.

title: Asking, and recording the refusal
detail: The audit's second finding was that no PF, ESI, TDS or PT is computed in a payroll run. The engine was never the problem - signed packs, JCS canonicalisation, effective-dated resolution, applicability with reason and evidence, a wage base assembled from declared component FLAGS rather than a list of component names, every figure carrying its rule and pack version so it can be re-derived years later. It was reachable from one screen and the payroll run never called it, so a closed month held no statutory lines and, worse, no record that the question had been asked. The run asks now. What it must never do is answer with the synthetic pack: jurisdiction IN-ZZ, authority 'this repository'. Wiring that through would have put a plausible made-up deduction on every payslip in the product and reduced somebody's net pay by it - the exact failure surface/Statutory.php's own docblock says the project refuses to commit. So a synthetic pack is a REASON, never a row, and what lands on the payslip is a sentence: PT was NOT computed and no PT line appears below, the pack in force is synthetic so it states no law and must not reduce anybody's net pay, the net here is the net before any PT, and what is missing is a signed pack from a named compliance owner rather than working code - until then the PT owed is UNKNOWN, not nil. The heads are discovered from whatever the installed packs declare, so a real pack adds PF and ESI with no code change. The test that carries the weight asserts a rupee figure: 35,283.87, identical with the statutory step and without it, checkable by hand as 6,00,000 over twelve, times 22 of 31 days, less the structure's one flat 200 - and separately proves the synthetic engine really would have produced 709.68 for that employment, which is the number that must never reach a payslip. Without that second assertion the first would pass against a zero wage base and prove nothing. Two deliberate breakages: letting the synthetic figure through failed 15 assertions, dropping the concerns from the merge failed 6. Separately, the float allow-list moved off file:line keys onto the text of the line. Line numbers had already broken twice in one afternoon - any edit above an allowed line renumbers it, the gate reports lines it was told to ignore, and the fix each time is to renumber entries without re-reading them, which is the ritual that turns an allow-list into a rubber stamp. Text keeps the property the line number was chosen for: change what the line does and it stops matching. Probed both ways - moved every line down three, still green; changed a 100 to a 99 inside an allowed line, one violation.

title: The two holes in the main loop
detail: The core HR loop had two gaps that a customer meets in the first week, and both are closed. PUNCHES FROM THE DEVICE. Every punch in this product was typed by a human, while the ported attendance_logs table carried device_sn, device_user_id, external_id and verify_mode and nothing had ever filled one - an attendance system is bought for exactly this. Not a device SDK: every biometric device in this market exports a delimited log, and that file is the universal interface. The column ORDER differs per vendor, so the layout is data in config/punch-layouts.json and is NAMED on every import rather than detected, because reading a ZKTeco file with an eSSL layout produces rows that parse perfectly and mean something else. The hard part was never parsing, it is that a device knows an enrolment number and not an employment: an id that maps to nobody is reported and NOT imported, and an id that maps to TWO employments is refused as ambiguous rather than resolved by picking one. An unmapped punch is somebody who worked and will not be paid; a mis-mapped one pays the wrong person; neither may be quiet. And re-importing the same file is the defect this class of tool always ships with, so a punch is identified by device, person, instant and direction - never by which file it arrived in - which also collapses the duplicate tail a device re-emits on a resumed export. Verified live through the screen: three punches, one already present, three unmapped ids named; the same file again imported nothing. LOANS AND ADVANCES NOW REACH A PAYSLIP. They were two CRUD screens and two outstanding reports, and Platform\Payroll\Recovery had sat finished and uncalled - the customer was told the recovery was manual, which means somebody types a deduction off a spreadsheet every month. The design decision that matters: the ported outstanding and balance columns are the OPENING figure and nothing writes to them. What has been recovered is derived from the closed runs, which are already append-only and never recomputed, so a reversed month reverses its recovery with it and a reversed instalment cannot leave a balance that is right by luck. The last instalment is the BALANCE and not the standing EMI - twelve times 4,000 against 47,500 takes 500 too much, and the employee is the one who has to notice. Verified live: a payslip printing 'instalment 1 of 12 against loan #7, 4,000.00 of 48,000.00, 44,000.00 outstanding after this one'. One more permission granted to nobody found on the way in: attendance.punch.ingest was in the catalogue and held by no role, which would have made the new screen a refusal for everybody including the administrator. That is the third time in this file, and it is now found by looking rather than by a sweep.

title: Forty-two megabytes to show fifty rows
detail: SqlStore::all() did SELECT * with no LIMIT and every list, picker, report and dashboard tile in the product went through it, paginating in PHP afterwards. Measured before touching anything, against the real attendance_logs shape: 40,000 rows is 0.51 seconds and 68 MB resident before PHP does anything with it, while the first page of fifty through SQL is 0.001 seconds and COUNT(*) is 0.005. A year of punches for two hundred staff is around half a million rows - roughly 850 MB, which is not a slow screen, it is a fatal error at the memory limit, on the biggest table, which is attendance, which is the thing an attendance system is bought for. The store now has a bounded read on the INTERFACE, so both implementations must provide it and neither can drift, and count() stopped being count(all()). The ORDER BY column is validated against the table's real columns and an unknown one is REFUSED rather than replaced with a default - a silent fallback means a screen that says it is sorted by date and is not. After the change the same 40,006 rows read as a page: 0.001 seconds, 0 MB. The most valuable test in the new file is not about speed at all: it puts the same rows through the JSON store and the SQL store and compares one store's answer against the other's, page by page, in both directions - because a difference between the two stores is the defect family this codebase keeps finding, and the file store agreeing with whatever you tell it is how five wrong column names survived for months. That test then caught something real, through the money gate: the file store's sort comparator compared numeric strings as FLOATS, and the columns it orders include ctc, which is DECIMAL(18,4). Eighteen significant digits, sixteen in a double. Demonstrated on this machine rather than argued: (float)'12345678901234.5678' <=> (float)'12345678901234.5679' is zero. Two different amounts reported equal, MySQL ordering them correctly, and the two stores therefore disagreeing about what page 2 contains - inside the very comparator whose job is to make the fallback behave like the real thing. It compares exact decimals now, no arithmetic, no bcmath dependency, with the one shape it does not handle (exponent notation) named rather than assumed away.

title: Fast until somebody uses it
detail: The remaining unbounded reads are closed. Search was the worst of them: the module list was bounded until somebody typed in the search box, at which point it read the whole table - fast until used, which is the worst possible arrangement. It is a WHERE over the module's declared search columns now, bounded and counted like the unsearched path, with the needle bound and % and _ escaped so somebody searching for '50%' gets the character rather than the table. Aggregates moved into SQL, and the money detail matters: SUM(ROUND(col,2)) per row and not ROUND(SUM(col),2), because Amount::of() rounds each stored figure to paise before adding and rounding once at the end is a different number - the fixture makes those differ on purpose (6000.03 against 6000.02) or the assertion would pass either way. SUM over a non-numeric column is refused rather than coerced, because a VARCHAR summed as zero is a total wrong by exactly the rows it could not read. Measured at 40,000 rows: search 0.277s/56MB became 0.034s/2MB, and the money sum 0.169s/56MB became 0.014s/2MB, cross-checked against the PHP loop it replaces at full scale rather than at seven rows. The decision worth recording is the lookup. Capping a dropdown at 500 is the obvious optimisation and, done plainly, it is worse than the bug: a picker silently showing 500 of 900 means somebody picks the wrong person or concludes an employee does not exist. So the cap states itself, the rows past it stay reachable by id, and validation on save moved off the truncated list onto the store - the 501st employee still saves, a nonexistent id is still refused, another tenant's id is still refused. The id box is named separately and declared to win, because two controls sharing one name is a silent trap where the browser sends both and whichever the server reads last quietly decides. Verified with 617 employees seeded: 502 options rendered, the truncation stated, an off-list employee saved correctly, a nonexistent id refused. The probe rows were removed and the counts checked back to 17 and 0.

title: The document that leaves the building
detail: A payslip is the one thing this product makes that goes outside it - to a bank for a loan, to a landlord, to the next employer, to a tribunal when something has gone wrong - and the only way to get one out was a browser print of the entire application: navy sidebar down the left, the search box, the sign-out button and the screen's own explanatory notes, across three sheets. Nobody hands that to a bank. The browser is the PDF writer. Every one of them has Save as PDF in its print dialog, and using it costs no dependency, no font licence, no server-side rendering step and no SECOND LAYOUT to keep in step with the first - which is what a PDF library would have been, and the second layout is always the one that drifts. So a print stylesheet, and a button on the payslip and on a rendered letter. Two decisions inside it worth recording. Concerns PRINT: the sentence saying a statutory head was not computed, or that this run is not approved, is coloured on screen, and dropping it from the printed copy because it is coloured would make the paper say less than the screen - and the person reading the paper is exactly the person who needs it. And table headers repeat across sheets while rows do not split, because a register that breaks a person across a page boundary is one somebody reads wrong. Verified: the button appears on a payslip and on a letter that rendered, and correctly does not appear on a letter that refused - the appointment letter for an employment with no reporting manager, where the placeholder refusal is doing its job.

title: Eighty-four screens behind one route
detail: Two pieces. First, sla_hours is read. Ten steps declare one, the field has always been editable, nothing had ever looked at it, and Platform\Workflow\Sla sat finished and uncalled - so Surface\Sla turns each open request's current step into the Node and Timer values the platform's own Sweep decides about. No second lateness calculation and no second idea of what 'stale' means: the breach time comes from the deadline rather than from when somebody looked, a stale timer is suppressed rather than acted on (a scheduler outage followed by a catch-up sweep must never approve a backlog), and reminders coalesce per approver. What still does not happen is anybody being TOLD, and the screens now say exactly that: the badge went from 'recorded only', which had become false, to 'reported, never sent', which does not become an overclaim later. A breach shown on a page somebody may not open is not an escalation. Second, 'complete all modules'. The first sweep I wrote reported all 84 broken, and it was wrong - it grepped for the word 'warning' and matched an HTML comment containing it, which is the same check-fails-on-its-own-documentation mistake the parse_ini_file guard made an hour earlier. Extending tools/smoke.php - the detector that already works, rather than a second weaker one - proved all 84 render clean, list and form, 226 visits. But rendering is the smaller half: a screen that renders and cannot save is the shape this product's defects keep taking. tools/modules-writable.php attempts a real insert through every module, in a transaction that is rolled back, and it found five whose forms rendered perfectly and answered a save with a raw SQLSTATE naming a constraint the person had never seen. Four were JSON columns rendered as free-text - MariaDB stores JSON as longtext with a json_valid CHECK, and the application account cannot read information_schema.CHECK_CONSTRAINTS, so the schema genuinely cannot say; widening its grants to find out would trade a real privilege boundary for a nicety, so the registry says it instead. The fifth was webhooks.last_received_at, declared as a number with a rupee sign in its label over a datetime column: a number box over a date, refused the moment anybody used it. That one generalised into a check that reads every declaration against the live schema and found four contradictions, three of them harmless (a checkbox over a varchar takes what the control posts) and reported as nothing, because flagging them would bury the one that mattered under three that did not. My probe was wrong twice on the way and both corrections are recorded in it: filling only the REQUIRED fields produced 52 false refusals, because 52 of the 84 modules declare nothing as required, and the two real findings would have been invisible among them.

title: The tool was changing what it measured
detail: Finishing the module proof turned up a defect in the proof itself, and it is the worst kind. tools/modules-writable.php prints 'Nothing was kept: every attempt ran in a transaction and was rolled back' at the end of every run. That sentence was false. The edit pass I added sat AFTER the finally that rolls the insert back, so it ran with no transaction open and COMMITTED - the tool had been writing a row into seventy-seven tables every time it ran. Reading the code did not find it; both times I read it, it looked right. Counting rows before and after a run found it in one command. And the residue did something worse than take up space: three modules that had refused on an earlier run began passing, because the rows the tool left behind gave their empty lookups something to point at. A tool for finding out whether the product works had started changing the answer, and the number it reported - 82 writable - was partly a measurement of itself. The honest figure with the 355 leaked rows removed is 80. So the promise is now checked rather than printed: tests/modules_rollback_test.php counts every table the registry names, runs the tool, and counts again, and it does not care how the tool is implemented - any future change that leaks a row fails there whatever it looks like on the page. Probed by reintroducing the exact defect (rollBack to commit): one failure, restored, green. The other half was worth having too. Every module now takes an insert AND an edit, because a module that accepts an insert and refuses an update is a screen where a typo is permanent, and the create and edit paths differ exactly where things go wrong. And the four JSON columns found earlier were not four: the schema was asked for every json_valid constraint it has, and the registry now declares each one it exposes rather than waiting to be told by the next person who types a word into a textarea over a JSON column. Eighty of eighty-four modules are writable and editable; the four that refuse do so correctly - the accounts table needs a tenant the generic engine must not invent, and three recruitment modules point at lookups with no rows to point at yet.

title: The pitch, at the place a customer meets it first
detail: A salary component could be one of five things: flat, percent of gross, percent of another component, the balance, or a schedule. A customer whose HRA is 'forty per cent of basic, capped at twenty thousand' could not say that - the single most common thing anybody asks of an HRA in this market - and it was a release. That is 'change configuration, not code' failing at the first place a customer touches it. Meanwhile Platform\Formula and its forty-one-class expression language sat finished, tested and called by nothing. They are wired now, and the seam went in two places for one reason each: SalaryComponent compiles and type-checks the expression in its CONSTRUCTOR, so every parse error, undeclared namespace, non-money result and missing rounding declaration becomes a refusal at PUBLISH, with a person present, rather than at half past two on the seventh; and PayslipCalculator builds the dependency graph in ITS constructor, so a cycle is refused before any amount exists. What an expression may read is decided and stated rather than left open - the month's gross, the components already computed this pass, payable and calendar days, and nothing else. No employee fields, no clock, no other employment: those are publish-time refusals rather than run-time nulls, and there is no NOW(), so November's recompute of March still gives March's answer. Two properties came free with the engine and are worth naming. Components are computed in TOPOLOGICAL order and printed in DECLARED order - SmartPRS 2 sorts by sequence and hard-codes five passes, so a customer who reorders their payslip changes their arithmetic. And rounding happens once, at the declared boundary, with exact rationals in between; there is no default rounding anywhere, so a component that declares an expression and no rounding_mode is refused rather than rounded the way somebody assumed. The worked example ships as a NEW effective-dated version from 2027-04-01, so nothing already computed moved: the 2026 version is byte-identical and every existing test figure still resolves to it. Proved end to end against the same input through both versions - gross 2,00,000 a month, full month: before, HRA 40,000; after, HRA 20,000 with the balance component absorbing the 20,000 so earnings still sum to gross and the net is unchanged at 1,99,800. And a run that cannot compute a component now THROWS rather than returning a payslip one line short, because a missing earning is somebody underpaid and on a payslip it looks exactly like a component nobody declared.

title: A surface with no session behind it
detail: Platform\Api was nine finished, tested classes and this product had no HTTP endpoint at all - so no integration, no mobile client, and no way for a biometric device's middleware to PUSH punches, which is the gap that actually costs sales. /api/v3 exists now: two reads and one write, and the write is punch ingest. Idempotency and the natural key divide the work on purpose - the idempotency key answers 'is this the same REQUEST twice', the punch's own identity answers 'is this the same PUNCH twice', and a client re-sending yesterday's export under a fresh key is duplicating rather than replaying, which only the data can see. The record is written in the same transaction as the effect, which is the engine's own rule: recording the key after a successful commit is not idempotent under a crash between the two - the money moved and nothing knows the key was used. What made this the riskiest thing built so far is that none of the accidental protection the rest of the product enjoys applies to it: no cookie, no CSRF token, no sign-in page. So the answers are deliberately uniform where a difference would be an oracle - one sentence for a missing, unknown, mistyped, revoked and expired credential, and the same 404 for an employment that does not exist and one belonging to another tenant, because a refusal that distinguishes them is an enumeration oracle wearing an access-control label. An unknown prefix still burns a hash verify so 'no such key' costs what 'wrong secret' costs. The tenant comes from the credential row and never from the request. And tools/api-sweep.php is in the standing suite with two POSITIVE controls, because 'the wrong scope is refused' is satisfied by an endpoint that refuses everybody. One real defect surfaced from wiring it. The API addresses an employment by its uuid rather than its integer id - the grammar's rule, because a sequential integer in a URL lets anyone who can count measure a headcount - and eighteen employments had no uuid. SqlStore stamps one on insert, but the SmartPRS 2 importer bypasses that, so every row of the owner's real imported history would have listed through the API and been addressable by nobody, for ever. The importer fills one now, tools/db/backfill-uuids.php fills the rows already there, and laragon-setup runs it straight after the import. The API had been reporting that state rather than falling back to the integer id, which is why it was findable at all.

title: A credential you cannot withdraw, and a front door that was not one
detail: Three loose ends, all of them the same shape: something that worked was not reachable, and something reachable was not the thing. Revoke first - the API Credentials screen could mint a bearer token that reads the employment list and writes attendance, and nothing on any screen could take it back. A key that cannot be withdrawn is a key for ever, which makes minting one a decision nobody can undo, and the single most likely reason to want the button is that the token has just left the building. It sets active = 0 rather than deleting the row, because the audit trail and last_used_at are how somebody answers what did that key do before we killed it, and a delete throws away the only copy of that answer at exactly the moment it matters. A second revoke refuses and says so - said rather than done again, because a repeat that reports success is one somebody trusts the first time without checking. An unknown id refuses too, and because the store is tenant-scoped that is also the honest answer for another tenant's key. Verified end to end: mint, 200 on /api/v3/employments, revoke, 401. Then the front door: visiting /SmartPRS3/public/ served a 1,871-line localhost-only development console, so the first thing a new machine showed was an internal tool and not the product. A bare visit now redirects to app.php; ?p= pages still work, because the console is genuinely useful and the fix is that it is not the entrance. Last, the README still opened by describing the repository as the first slice of the platform - platform primitives and foundation schema - which stopped being true a long time ago and was the first paragraph anybody read. Replaced with what it now is, how to run it, and a table of where things live. Skipped: the OpenAPI document. A spec needs schema definitions that do not exist, and inventing them so a generator has something to print is ceremony that would be wrong within a week.

title: The rule engine had no door, and the rule it replaces was one line of PHP
detail: Platform\Rules is twenty-five finished, tested classes and nothing a user could open had ever entered it. Meanwhile Surface\Attendance decided what a day was worth with workedMinutes > 0, and its own comment admitted the debt - that threshold is a policy decision and in the real product it is a rule the tenant publishes. A rule engine nobody can reach and a business rule hard-coded beside it are the same defect seen from two sides, and fixing either one alone fixes neither. config/attendance-rules.json now declares five rules for attendance.day.classify and Surface\DayRules hands them to the real Engine, with real SPX in every condition, parsed against the decision point's real symbol table. The bridge is deliberately thin: nothing in it re-implements matching, ordering or conflict, because a second rule engine is always the one that gets it wrong. Two things it refuses to do. It does not fall back to PRESENT - a missing file, an unparseable rule and no match all return UNCLASSIFIED with the reason printed, because a classifier that fails to a status pays a month of absences in full and looks entirely normal doing it. And one bad rule publishes NONE of them rather than the four that still parse, because a rule set that silently shrinks is how a typo removes the full-day rule and makes everybody half-present. The status on the screen carries the winning rule's code and its business description, and the full decision - every candidate, why each lost - opens under the table. The rule that earns its keep is ATT-OPEN-SHIFT: an in-punch with no out-punch is HALF_DAY and flagged, not ABSENT. The person was demonstrably at work; what is missing is a punch, not a day, and SmartPRS 2 pays it as a full absence, which is the largest single source of attendance disputes because the correction lands after the payslip. On the demo data that is exactly the day that shows. NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: payableDays() still counts workedMinutes > 0. Feeding a HALF_DAY into payroll changes what a payslip pays, and quietly changing the input to money in the same turn as wiring a new engine is the shape of the bug that made every payslip twelve times too high. It is the next decision, taken deliberately.

title: The analyser was pointed at the easy half, and found 127 checks that check nothing
detail: composer install landed on the owner's machine, so phpstan and deptrac could finally run. Staging phpstan.phar into the sandbox made the first half of that possible here. Two things came out of it and the second is the point. First: phpstan.neon listed src, database, tests and tools in `paths` and NOT surface or public - so everything it had ever looked at was the pure, typed platform, and none of the forty classes and two front controllers that run when somebody opens the product. That is the identical mistake the four law gates made when they were rooted at src/, which cost fifty violations the day they were re-pointed; an analyser aimed away from the risk is a check that checks the easy half. Second, and this is why the run was worth it: with surface and public included the first pass reported 11,412 findings, of which 127 were the class this codebase cares about most - a comparison that can never be true, a variable that might not be defined, a ?-> on something never null, an instanceof the type system already guarantees. Every one of those is a check that silently checks nothing, found mechanically instead of by somebody noticing. All 127 are fixed. What they turned out to be: a test regex written \$route inside double quotes, so it interpolated an undefined variable and matched ANY comparison rather than the one it named; phase3's exit gate comparing ValueCoercion::FILE_DATE_FORMAT against the literal 'd-m-Y' and then testing for the literal, so changing the constant would have left the gate checking a stale string for ever; a tautology asserting PASSWORD_FLOOR < 12 OR >= 12; an assertion that count(ENTRIES) === 14 with both sides constant-folded; and thirteen undefined-variable findings in phase5 criteria, now a real refusal rather than a confusing later error. The largest group was a pattern worth naming: a narrow docblock DISABLING A RUNTIME GUARD. AmountRouter::select declared list<array{from: ?int, to: ?int}> and then checked is_int on each boundary - and because treatPhpDocTypesAsCertain is on, the docblock had quietly proved the guard dead. Bands arrive from JSON, where "from": 50000.0 is what a real file contains. A guard at a trust boundary that a type annotation has disproved is the worst of both worlds: it looks like a check, it costs a branch, and the analyser has been told to stop believing the input can be wrong. Nine of those were found and the fix in every case was to widen the declaration to what actually arrives, never to delete the guard. Two findings are kept deliberately and argued in ignoreErrors with reasons: a divide-by-zero guard on money that phpstan proves unreachable (a redundant comparison costs one branch, a missing one costs a DivisionByZeroError on a payroll report), and a register-direction check that cannot fire for today's constants and fires the day somebody adds a fourth direction. The remaining ~8,400 are level-9 mixed propagation on an untyped-row architecture - the same true observation restated thousands of times - and they are ledgered in a baseline, with the always-wrong class explicitly excluded from it so a new one turns check.php red the same day. The baseline has to be generated on the machine that has vendor/: the sandbox has no laravel/framework, so 2,900 of its findings are class-not-found for classes that exist perfectly well on a real install. Also fixed: composer.json's psr-4 mapped SmartPRS\\ to src/ and nothing to surface/, so every one of the forty Surface classes was invisible to the composer autoloader - harmless today because app.php registers its own, and a silent hole the first time anything uses composer's.

title: Half a day, all the way to the payslip - and an int that would have rounded it in silence
detail: The rule engine could say HALF_DAY and nothing downstream could hear it. payableDays() still counted workedMinutes > 0, PayslipCalculator::calculate() took `int $payableDays`, settlements.payable_days was INT(11), and four screens printed `(int) $row['payable_days']`. Every one of those would have taken 17.5 and reported 17 or 18 without a word - MySQL does not refuse a decimal into an INT, an int cast does not warn, and a screen showing 17 next to the word PAID looks exactly like a screen showing the truth. So: config/attendance-rules.json now declares what each status is worth in HALVES of a day (a day is 2, half a day is 1) because 0.5 is a float and law 7 says money is exact; the arithmetic stays in whole numbers to the last step. PayslipCalculator takes a Rational in days - 17 and a half is 35/2 - and the guard, the trace, the full-month comparison and the SPX context all move with it. Rational gained toDecimalString(), which truncates rather than rounds, because a display that rounds 17.499 up next to a payslip is one somebody reconciles against. settlements.payable_days is DECIMAL(6,2) by migration 000600. A status the policy does not price is REPORTED as unpriced and counts for nothing, rather than being defaulted in either direction: guessing high pays for a month nobody worked and guessing low withholds pay, and neither shows anywhere. Attendance::payableDays() now reads the same rules file PayrollPeriod does, so the attendance screen and the payroll screen cannot disagree about what a day is worth - which matters more than either being right, because two screens computing one fact two ways is how they drift and the one somebody trusts is whichever they opened first. On the demo data both now say 0.5 where attendance used to say 0: the day with an in-punch and no out-punch. AND THE THING THAT FELL OUT OF IT. Writing the migration exposed that tools/db/migrate.php re-seeds the founding tenant whenever ANY migration is applied. That worked for as long as every run started from an empty database. 000600 is the first migration ever ADDED to an already-migrated one, and it applied, recorded itself, and then died on a duplicate tenant uuid - so laragon-setup.bat would have read the non-zero exit and stopped with 'Migrate refused' on a database whose schema was in fact perfectly up to date. Every future migration would have done that to every existing install. The seed now asks the database whether it has a tenant instead of inferring it from the count of migrations applied, which was never the same question.

title: The hardest checks in the project were not in the command that runs the checks
detail: The phase exit gates prove the money is right, the packs resolve by statutory date and the traces reproduce - and none of them was in `php tools/check.php`. They ran when somebody remembered. Two consequences were true at the same time and neither was visible from anywhere. Phase 5 had been FAILING, on criterion 3: no component name appears as a literal. `public/app.php` computed statutory contributions with `compute('PT', ...)` and `public/index.php` declared applicability the same way, which is law 1's business literal sitting in the two files the whole argument is about - and it was doing real harm beyond the principle, because the payroll screen showed exactly ONE statutory head for ever, so the day a real pack brings PF, ESI and TDS the screen would still have shown professional tax with nothing to say the others existed. It now asks the packs which heads are in force, across every date it probes rather than only today (the first version asked only the period end, and the second probe date exists precisely because the pack is in force then and not now, so the table emptied itself and claimed no head was declared). No head in force is a NAMED state, because 'nothing is declared' and 'nothing was computed' look identical on a blank screen and mean opposite things to somebody deciding whether payroll is safe to run. The second consequence was mine: changing PayslipCalculator's signature fatally broke tools/phase5/criteria.php, and the full standing suite stayed green through it. So tools/phase-gates.php now runs all eleven and sits in check.php. Its only real logic is keeping FAILED apart from NOT PROVEN: a gate exits non-zero for both and they mean opposite things - failed is a defect here, not proven is a fact about the world this repository cannot supply, phase 6 waiting on a named compliance owner and phase 10 on a customer's numbers and phase 0 on business decisions only the owner can answer. Failing the suite on those would make it permanently red, and a permanently red suite is one people stop reading; they are reported every run instead. Two things it got wrong first, both worth keeping: reading the verdict as the last line of output filed phase 0 as failed, because its verdict wraps onto a second line of prose - it now scans backwards for a line that looks like a verdict; and the held-detection checks that the arithmetic adds up (every criterion not proven is accounted for) so a gate cannot hide a real failure behind a held one. Proven non-vacuous by breaking phase 4 and watching the suite go red.

title: Leave had no balance check at all, and a second rules file found the bridge's bug
detail: Surface\Leave::request() validated two things: that the dates spanned at least one day, and that a reason was typed. Not the balance. An employee with three days of earned leave could ask for forty; the row was written, it joined the approvals queue looking exactly like every other request, and the only thing between it and a negative balance was an approver noticing something the screen does not show them. config/leave-rules.json now declares three rules at leave.request.validate - more days than the balance holds, more than the balance LESS the days already committed to other pending requests (without which an employee with five days submits five five-day requests, each passing on its own), and a supporting document over three days. Refused BEFORE the write, because a request that exists and should not is now something somebody has to withdraw. The screen and the writer call the same validate(), so a form cannot offer a button and then refuse the submission. WRITING THE SECOND RULES FILE IS WHAT MADE THE FIRST ONE HONEST. DayRules had a hundred lines of file-to-engine bridge inline; the choice was to copy them or lift them, and a second copy of a bridge is a second set of failure modes to be discovered twice. Surface\PublishedRules is that lift, taken at the second consumer and not before - one caller never tells you which parts are general, and the part that turned out NOT to be is the interesting half: what to do with the actions the engine emits is entirely the caller's business, so the bridge stops at handing back the EvaluationResult and never interprets one. Lifting it immediately exposed a defect the single caller had hidden. The bridge defaulted every rule's conflict policy to HighestPriorityOnly and read an `on_conflict` key out of the JSON, so config/leave-rules.json could declare "policy": "all_match" at the top, be believed by everyone reading it, and evaluate as highest-priority-only - a request over its balance reported the balance and said nothing about the document it also needed. The policy is the DECISION POINT'S, and DecisionPoints::conflictPolicy() is where that fact lives; a copy of it in a config file is a copy that can disagree, and for an afternoon the copy that was believed was the wrong one. The declaration is gone from the file. Two smaller things the engine taught: leave.balance is a KEYED accessor, so the rules ask leave.balance(leave.type) and the caller supplies the value under the rendered key - writing the bare name resolves to nothing and poisons the comparison rather than passing it; and a Leave built with no rules now refuses and says nothing checked the request, which broke write_paths_test until it was given the rules the application gives it. That break is the design working: the safe reading of 'the policy did not load' is not 'there is no policy'.

title: Two statuses that were priced and could never happen
detail: config/attendance-rules.json has valued WEEKLY_OFF and HOLIDAY at a full day of pay since the file was written, and NOTHING could ever produce either. The two symbols that decide it - day.is_weekly_off and day.is_holiday - were not among the values handed to the engine, so no rule could read them and none was written. The table read as configured, every check walked past an entry that was there, and the effect was that a Sunday with no punches came out ABSENT. That is the same defect as a permission sitting in the catalogue that no role holds, which this codebase has now found four times, and it is worth naming as a pattern: a declaration is not a capability, and the thing that makes it look like one is that the declaration is where anybody would look. The working calendar is now handed to the classifier and two rules read it - a holiday outranks a weekly off, because a holiday landing on a Sunday is still the answer somebody wants when they ask why the day was paid, and both outrank every punch-counting rule, because somebody who comes in on their day off has worked and the day was still not a working day. Absent a calendar the two symbols are NULL rather than false: a rule asking about a weekly off then produces an unknown and poisons its own condition, instead of quietly answering no. Saying 'this was not a holiday' when nothing knows the holiday list is a lie with a payslip attached. Also taken out of code: graceMinutes: 5, written into the ShiftWindow constructor call in Surface\Attendance where it looked like a harmless default and was in fact the policy that decides whether somebody is marked late - which in most Indian attendance policies is the first step towards a day of loss of pay. It comes from config/calendar.json now, and the fallback when a file does not say is a NAMED constant rather than a literal in an argument list, so reading the class tells you a default is being applied. One near-miss worth recording: $calendar was constructed EIGHT LINES AFTER the Attendance it was being passed to, so PHP would have handed over an undefined variable as null without a word - and null is a meaning here, not an absence. Every Sunday would have come out ABSENT and the only visible symptom would have been a smaller payroll.

title: Overtime was computed on every page load and read by nobody
detail: Platform\Attendance\DaySettlement has produced overtimeMinutes for every settled day since Phase 4. The attendance screen printed it in a column. No comp-off was ever credited, no overtime was ever recorded, and no rule could have said otherwise because attendance.day.earn had no rules published against it at all. A figure computed on every render and consumed by nobody is not a feature; it is a number that makes a screen look finished. config/attendance-earn-rules.json now credits a comp-off for a full shift worked on a weekly off, another for one worked on a declared holiday - kept as two rules rather than an OR, because plenty of employers pay for the holiday and give time back for the weekend, and one rule doing both cannot be changed independently - and records overtime past the shift on an ordinary working day. RECORDED, not paid: nothing in this build declares an overtime multiplier and a rule emitting an amount would be inventing one, so the parameter says OT-NOT-DECLARED and the screen says 'recorded, not priced'. THE BUG THE SECOND DECISION POINT FOUND. PublishedRules passed every action parameter through as a literal, and Action::resolve() only evaluates Expression instances - so `"minutes": "attendance.ot_minutes"` would have written the NAME of the symbol into an overtime entry as its value, silently, on a screen where it reads as a plausible label. A parameter now says when it is an expression: {"expr": "..."} is parsed and resolved, anything else is a literal. Explicit rather than sniffed, because the first thing a 'does this look like SPX' guess gets wrong is a reason written in English that happens to parse. TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY SEPARATED. Reading what a day earned and crediting it are different acts: classification runs on every page load, so a screen that credited while rendering would credit once per refresh - the accrual defect this codebase has already fixed once, and far harder to notice the second time because nobody watches a comp-off balance the way they watch a leave balance. postEarnings() is a button, idempotent by the day's own identity (comp-off:2026-09-06), and re-posting a wider range that contains an already-credited day posts nothing. LeaveLedger gained an EARNED kind rather than filing comp-offs as ADJUSTMENT: a statement is read by the person it belongs to, and 'adjustment' says somebody changed something where 'earned' says why they have the day. The credit is REFUSED for a leave type config/leave-policy.json does not declare - a balance no screen shows and no payroll spends is not a smaller feature, it is a day somebody earned and cannot find. Verified end to end on a live screen: a Sunday classified WEEKLY_OFF, earning one day of CO, credited once, second press credited nothing.

title: Three late arrivals cost half a day, and a string that was a float in disguise
detail: attendance.late_minutes has been computed for every settled day since Phase 4 and, exactly like overtime, nothing ever read it: somebody could be forty minutes late every morning of the month and the payslip would not know. SmartPRS 2 does have this rule, in PayrollGenController::attendanceCut():449-455, as a loop with the numbers written into it - which is why 'we give fifteen minutes, not ten' is a release there and a line in config/attendance-penalty-rules.json here. RL-ATT-001 is now published, the deduction reaches the payable figure, and the working prints every day it charged for and the rule that charged. THE COUNTER IS PREPARED, NEVER QUERIED, and that contract earned its keep twice in one afternoon. The engine holds no repository by design, so a rule counting late arrivals over a payroll month reads a value the caller assembled under a canonical key (§5.9) - and the first attempt supplied a bare int, which arrives with no SPX type. The rule failed ERR_TYPE, loudly, naming the symbol; the alternative design, where an unprepared counter reads as zero, would have forgiven every late arrival in the product silently and nothing on any screen would have said so. There is a test asserting exactly that: strip the key and the evaluation must REPORT rather than answer. THE ONE THAT WOULD HAVE COST MONEY. The engine canonicalises a resolved action parameter, so `0.5d` comes back as the STRING "1/2" - and the first version of the loop wrote (int) round((float) $fraction * 2). (float) "1/2" is 1.0. Half a day became a whole day, on the number subtracted from somebody's gross, under a trace that read perfectly at every step. That is law 7 in one line: a float anywhere near money is a defect, and a cast through a string is a float wearing a disguise. The repair was not at the call site: Rational could WRITE "1/2" and could not READ it, and a serialisation a class emits and cannot parse is an invitation to exactly that cast. Rational::parse() closes the round trip and refuses anything it did not write. PenaltyRules also refuses a penalty that is not a whole number of half-days rather than rounding it, because rounding a penalty is choosing, silently, which way somebody loses. Two smaller decisions recorded: the penalty grace (10 minutes) is deliberately NOT the same number as calendar.grace_minutes (5) - an employer can mark somebody late at five and only start charging at ten, and collapsing the two takes that choice away; and the payable figure is floored at zero, because a month of nothing but penalties would otherwise produce a negative that PayslipCalculator correctly refuses, leaving a screen that cannot render instead of one that says the month is worth nothing. Verified live: three late mornings, 1.5 days deducted, every charged day named on the screen.

title: A holiday inside a leave span was charged, and an unknown that quietly said yes
detail: Surface\Leave::workingDaysBetween() counted a request's days with `(int) $day->format('N') <= 5`. Monday to Friday, in PHP, ignoring the working calendar entirely. Two consequences, and the first is the commonest leave complaint there is: A HOLIDAY INSIDE THE SPAN WAS CHARGED, so somebody who took the week of a festival paid for the festival out of their own balance. And a tenant whose weekly off is Sunday only got Saturdays free, because the code's idea of a week was not theirs. config/leave-charge-rules.json now decides it at leave.request.charge against the same working calendar the attendance rules read, so the two halves of the product cannot disagree about which days are working days. An exempted day is stated as its own EXEMPT_DAY with a reason rather than left as the absence of a charge: 'this day was exempted, here is why' and 'no rule mentioned this day' are different answers and only one can be argued with. The count feeds the balance check too - what a request is REFUSED on has to be the number it would actually be charged, or a week containing a holiday is rejected on a figure nobody would ever pay. THE FINDING THAT MATTERED MORE THAN THE FEATURE. The first version supplied NULL for day.is_weekly_off and day.is_holiday when no calendar was given, on the theory that SPX's three-valued logic would then refuse to answer. It refuses for a `when` and it does NOT refuse for an `except`: an unknown `except` carves nothing out, so the rule it guards fires anyway. Every day of every span was charged at full price, with a trace saying 'null' in small print. That is a fail-open on somebody's leave balance and it only ever errs one way. Then the same shape turned up in attendance, pointing the other way: with no calendar the two rules reading those symbols do not match and every rule BELOW them fires normally, so a Sunday with no punches classifies ABSENT instead of WEEKLY_OFF - a full day of pay gone because nobody loaded a holiday list. Omitting the symbols instead of nulling them changes nothing; an absent declared symbol is unknown, not an error. Both are fixed the same way and it is the same discipline the prepared aggregation counters already enforce: A QUESTION THE CALLER CANNOT SUPPLY THE INPUTS FOR IS NOT A QUESTION TO ASK. ChargeRules refuses the whole span, Attendance refuses to classify at all, both report the reason, and payableDays() counts the days as unpriced on the screen. Loud and wrong beats quiet and wrong. workingDaysBetween() survives as a NAMED fallback that says on the screen exactly what it did instead - a wrong answer that announces itself is recoverable.

title: The product decided somebody's leave and told them nothing
detail: Platform\Notification\Outbox has had a careful contract since Phase 8 - queued, sent, delivered, and delivered ONLY on a provider acknowledgement, because marking delivered when an API call returns 200 is how a payroll team believes four hundred payslip notifications went out on the 1st when the gateway dropped every one. Nothing had ever queued a message into it. An employee found out their leave was rejected by opening the screen and looking, which is what SmartPRS 2 does and is the reason its customers ask for an app. config/notifications.json declares what each event says, to whom, on which channels; Surface\Notifications queues into the ported notification_log table (no migration needed - SmartPRS 2's own table already carries kind, title, body, channels, dedupe_key and email_status); Leave::decide() queues one; the inbox shows the queue. NOTHING IS TRANSMITTED, AND THAT IS THE DECISION. No SMTP server, no SMS gateway, no push provider is configured, and none is invented: mail() against an unconfigured host returns true on plenty of systems, which would mark messages SENT that nobody received - the exact failure Outbox exists to make impossible. Every row is QUEUED, the config file says so in its own transport block, the screen says so in red above the table, and there is an assertion whose only job is that the state is never anything else. Four smaller decisions worth keeping. REDACTED ON THE WAY IN, through the platform's own Redactor, and `leaking()` asks the STORE rather than an in-memory outbox - a redaction proved only against objects in memory is proved against the one copy nobody can read anyway, and the database, the backup and the support export are what actually get read. IDEMPOTENT BY DEDUPE KEY on the request id, because four copies of one rejection is the version of this failure that reaches the founder. AN UNDECLARED EVENT IS REFUSED rather than improvised from its code, which would send a customer something nobody wrote. And the queue call is in a try/catch that does NOT swallow: the leave is already decided and the ledger has already moved, so throwing would leave a person unable to see a decision that has happened - but the failure is carried back on the row so a screen can say somebody was not told, because deciding quietly and not telling quietly are the two halves of the same defect.

title: Four publish gates refused the shipped workflow file, and every one was right
detail: Platform\Workflow has parallel nodes, quorum, SLA timers, delegation, escalation and a Validator with eleven publish gates, and nothing on any screen had ever entered it - the note in config/workflows.json has said so honestly since somebody noticed it claimed otherwise. Surface\PublishedWorkflows now COMPILES every declaration into a real WorkflowDefinition and runs the gates against it. The compiling is the easy half; what made this worth doing is that the gates refused the shipped file four times in a row and each refusal was a defect in my compiler, not in them. W03: an approval node produces FIVE outcomes, not two - approved, rejected, returned, escalated, auto_decided - and the three nobody thinks about are exactly what strands a request. A request sitting at a node with no transition for the outcome it just produced is somebody's leave, or somebody's money, frozen with no screen able to say why. W14: I ended each chain with auto_approve nodes, and the gate said no path reaches a FINALISE node - a workflow that cannot complete is not a workflow. An auto-approve node is a step that decides; a finalise node is the end, and a graph whose end is a step never ends. W05: routing `returned` and `escalated` back to the node that produced them is a cycle with no return_for_edit or escalate node in it - an approval loop with no human-visible return is an infinite loop, and a request bouncing between an approver and themselves is one nobody can see moving. So the compiler now derives a real `sent_back` node of the platform's return_for_edit type, and one escalate node per approval that routes UP the chain, because escalation means the person above decides and a single shared escalate node would not know which step it came from. W11: both of those then had no participant, and a task node with no participant 'can only ever fail the instance' - a returned request assigned to nobody dies the moment it is sent back, which an employee would report as 'my leave disappeared'. All five declared chains now compile and pass all eleven gates, the requests screen shows it, and a chain that would strand a request is named with the gate that refuses it and why. NOT DONE, AND SAID SO: instances still run through Surface\Requests' linear chain. Validating what is declared is the prerequisite for running it, not a stepping stone dressed as one - SmartPRS 2 has no equivalent check at all, and a chain there is whatever the controller happens to do.

title: Two Print buttons, and no print stylesheet at all
detail: public/app.php carried two buttons marked `class="no-print"` and there was NO @media print block anywhere in the file, so the class styled nothing. Both Surface\Payslip and Surface\Letters carry a ponytail: comment saying a PDF writer is deferred and the browser prints in the meantime - and the meantime had never been made to work. What that button produced was the payslip with the navy sidebar, the search box and the button itself; and, found by actually rendering one through wkhtmltopdf rather than by reading the markup, THE STANDING INSTALLATION WARNINGS: 'a default credential is present on this installation' and 'password floor lowered to 8 characters', printed above somebody's net pay, on the document they file with a bank and hand to a landlord. Embarrassing, and a description of the system's weak points posted to everybody who gets paid. NO PDF LIBRARY IS ADDED AND NONE IS NEEDED. vendor/ carries no dompdf, TCPDF or mPDF; adding one is a dependency the customer installs, a font licence to think about, and a SECOND LAYOUT to keep in step with the first - and the second layout is always the one that drifts, and the day it drifts an employee's filed copy stops matching the register. Every browser prints to PDF. The lazy correct answer is a stylesheet that makes what it prints correct: A4 with margins, the application stripped, ink rather than screen colours, no table row split across two pages, and one payslip per page. AND THE BATCH, because the per-employee screen is not the workflow. A payroll team produces four hundred payslips and doing that one Ctrl+P at a time is the reason people ask for a PDF library; ?r=payslips-batch renders a whole closed run, one per page, so a single print produces the month as one file. It reads each payslip through the same Payslip::from() against the same stored run as the individual screen - deliberately not a second renderer - and narrows through Scope::only(), because a batch print is the widest read in the product: every salary in the tenant on one page. An employment in the run that produces no payslip is NAMED above the pages rather than dropped, since a batch that silently prints 397 of 400 is a batch nobody counts. The route was picked up automatically by the standing sweeps - 31 routes now, 248 scope visits, 0 leaking - which is the sweeps doing exactly what they were built for.

title: The employees table has a joining date and no exit date at all
detail: `employees` carries doj, status and employment_stage and NO EXIT DATE. The product knew somebody had left and did not know when - which is exactly the shape Platform\Lifecycle\EmploymentTimeline was written against, four finished and tested classes nothing on any screen had ever called, whose own docblock names the consequence: SmartPRS 2 'issues a payslip for somebody who left in March because leaving is a flag rather than an event with a date'. There is now an employment_events table, a Surface\Timeline that persists it, a card on the attendance screen that records and shows it, and - the reason for all of it - a payroll period that REFUSES a month beginning after somebody exited and prorates the month they left in. A device that keeps sending punches, a row imported twice or a badge somebody else is using does not know the person has gone; the timeline does. A COLUMN PER EVENT IS THE OTHER WRONG ANSWER and it is the one that looks tidier. confirmed_on, promoted_on, exited_on answers 'when did they leave' and cannot answer 'what was their grade in August?' - a column holds today's value, a timeline holds what was true on a date - and it cannot hold two transfers. NOT probation_events, which already exists with exactly these columns: employee_id / action / details / effective / by / at is a generic dated event log wearing one event's name, and reusing it would have cost nothing today and left every future reader of the schema believing the exits in it were something to do with probation. SILENCE IS NOT AN ANSWER, and that is the assertion that took the most care. Most employments in a ported database have no events yet; reading an empty timeline as 'not employed' would have stopped every payslip in the tenant on the day this shipped. activeOn() returns NULL for a timeline with nothing on it and the caller is left to decide. TWO THINGS FELL OUT OF IT. The app account holds table-by-table grants (Law 2), so a table a migration just created is INVISIBLE to it - information_schema only shows a table to an account with some privilege on it - and the symptom is a fatal naming a table that plainly exists. laragon-setup.bat runs the grant step straight after migrate for that reason; migrate on its own did not say so, and now it does. And two tests carry deliberate table-count canaries (171 tables, 149 tenant-scoped) that this migration correctly broke: they are meant to need changing, because a schema that grows without anybody noticing is how SmartPRS 2 ended up with 39 tables created at runtime inside controllers.
