REGRESSION: light mode rendered before and after against identical markup differs by 1,098 pixels of 1,800,000, all inside one 34x34 box — the topbar avatar, the deliberate gradient fix above. Precedence verified live: company gold -> pick Plum -> #9333ea -> back to Company -> gold -> custom #00a3a3 -> reset -> gold. Reload keeps the choice. The change to app.php is purely additive: three insertions, zero lines removed.

title: composer check: 61 gate violations triaged to zero, six of them real
detail:
First `composer check` since 18 Sep, so five days had accumulated. 61 violations, NONE from the theme change committed earlier the same day — verified by mapping every reported line against the three inserted regions (difflib), not assumed.

44 were surface/IdCardPdf.php and surface/Sheet.php: a hand-written CR80 PDF writer (242.65 x 153.01 POINTS) whose floats are glyph advances, point sizes, x/y/w/h and ellipse control points, and one Excel serial date guarded by Date::isDateTime(). Neither file handles money at all. 11 more were public/app.php: capDecimals() (display rounding for a decimal(10,4) radius/lat-lng/rate, which its own docblock rules money out of), the dashboard donut (the `else` of `elseif ($panel['money'])`, so only ever a count), leave day balances and a KPI percentage. All suppressed by line TEXT in tools/gates/allow/floats.php with a reason each, so all 60 stay counted and printed. That file's `notes` claimed surface/ should carry no entry; it predates both files and was rewritten rather than deleted, keeping the standard it set.

1 was strict-types on public/diag.php (a disabled 5-line stub) and 1 was a gate:allow-swallow annotation on a catch that does not swallow — it assigns an empty org graph, which is the answer, not the absence of one. Annotation removed, reasoning kept as a plain comment.
found: is_numeric() guarded the CTC (LPA) box and accepts "1e3", which casts to 1000 — a three-character typo previewed a payslip priced at 10 crore, with no refusal and a trace that checked out. This is the defect the Law 7 gate actually caught; the float arithmetic beside it never produced a wrong figure.
got_wrong_first: Read the dashboard donut legend as a real Law 7 display defect — the bar view prints $rupees($row['value']) and the donut prints number_format((float) ...), and the donut's own comment claims the legend figure is exact. Was about to report it as a bug. It is the `else` branch of `elseif ($panel['money'])`, so the donut is only ever drawn for a count and the comment is right. Checked the branch structure before writing it up.
checks: The gate was reproduced locally against the real files so every suppression key was generated with the gate's own normaliser and verified to match, rather than hand-written. Before: 61. After: no-float-money 0/60 suppressed, no-empty-catch 0/17, strict-types 0/0.

title: CTC <-> LPA is exact (Law 7), and is a named method
detail:
Employment gains annualFromLpa(), lpaOrNull() and ctcAsLpa(), and the two front-controller sites call them. A NAMED METHOD for the reason monthlyGross()'s docblock already gives: a `/ 12` loose in the register made every payslip twelve times too high with a correct-looking trace under each figure, and a `* 100000` loose in public/app.php is the same bet.

annualFromLpa() takes string|Rational so a caller that already parsed the box hands the Rational straight over rather than rendering it back to a string to re-parse. ctcAsLpa() rounds HalfUp to four places rather than using Rational::toDecimalString()'s truncation, deliberately: truncating moved the fourth decimal down on roughly one real CTC in three (Rs 1,04,166.67 annual read 1.0416 where it had always read 1.0417). Exactness was the point; moving a figure an owner recognises was not.
found: The float arithmetic here was LATENT, not live: number_format(..., 2) rounded the error away before Money::of() saw it, and across 50,000 LPA values and 8,930 CTC comparisons old and new agree on every one. Law 7 is absolute because the SmartPRS 2 instalment defect was latent too.
got_wrong_first: Wrote rtrim(rtrim($lpa, '0'), '.') to strip trailing zeros without reading Rational::toDecimalString() to the end — it already strips them AND omits the point entirely for a whole number, so that rtrim turns the exact string "100" into "1". A round Rs 1,00,00,000 would have prefilled the box with 1 LPA. Five of the test's own expectations were also wrong on the first run; the implementation was right each time.
checks: tests/ctc_lpa_test.php, 20 assertions, green. Confirmed it FAILS against the old implementation for the right reason: 3 guard assertions ('1e3', '.5', ' 12.5 ' all pass is_numeric). Behaviour identical on both screens: 50,000 preview values and 8,930 prefill comparisons.

title: Attendance: "Muster" is now Attendance status, and the punches got a Log button
detail:
Owner asked for: the word 'muster' replaced, a Log column at the end of the grid opening an employee's days with login/logout/break/late and an export, and a new 'Attendance Logs' menu item under Attendance Report showing one row per employee-day with First IN / Last Out / IN / OUT / Late Minutes / Break / Shift / Emp ID / Name / Branch / Team Lead, a per-row Log button and an export.

MOST OF THIS ALREADY EXISTED and the change is mostly config. The report's 'Daily rows' view is exactly the requested screen — AttendanceReport::daily() already returns every one of those columns, config/attendance-report.json already declares them, and the `daily-attendance` alias route already opened it with v=daily. It was simply called 'Daily Attendance' and sat ABOVE Attendance Report in the menu. So it is renamed 'Attendance Logs' and moved below Attendance Report in config/navigation.json — a rename and a reorder, no new screen. Building a third view would have put two identical screens in one menu.

The route KEY stays `daily-attendance`: renaming it would break every bookmark and link written against it for a word nobody sees. The page title follows the nav label automatically (the title is read from the nav item matching $rawRoute), and the screen now varies its own heading on $mIsLogs = $rawRoute === 'daily-attendance'.

Actually new: (1) 'Muster' -> 'Attendance status' on the grid heading, the page subtitle and the export filename; (2) a Log column at the END of the grid, one button per employee, opening Attendance Logs filtered to that person and period — the grid's cells already opened ONE day, this is the whole range; (3) the `logs` column on the daily view rendered as a Log button instead of the inline string '09:02 in · 13:31 out · 14:06 in · 18:44 out', which was unreadable at four pairs and pushed every later column off screen — the string is now the button's tooltip and the button opens that day in full; (4) AttendanceReport::dayCsv() + a `muster-day-csv` action, so the per-day drill-down can be exported.
found: The per-day drill-down was the ONLY view in this report with nothing to export, and it is the one somebody attaches to a regularisation email — it had to be retyped or screenshotted.

config/attendance-report.json declares `late_minutes` default:false, so the requested Late Minutes column is off on a fresh install. Flipped to true. NOTE this does not affect an install that has already saved a column choice: columns() reads the tenant's saved list with in_array() and ignores the shipped default entirely, so on THIS install Late By (min) must be ticked on Configuration -> Attendance report. That is the owner's own rule (on-screen setting, never a file edit) working as intended, not a bug.
got_wrong_first: Was about to build 'Attendance Logs' as a new route and screen before checking the nav config, which would have shipped a second copy of the Daily rows view sitting two items apart from the first in the same menu. The `daily-attendance` alias at the top of app.php and nav item 0 are what stopped it.
checks: php -l on app.php and AttendanceReport.php; both JSON configs re-parse. Diff on app.php removes exactly the 8 lines it replaces and nothing else. tests/attendance_log_csv_test.php (8 assertions) covers dayCsv: a break belongs to the session it PRECEDES and the first session exports an empty cell rather than 0 (nobody took a nought-minute break), an unpaired punch is listed in the column matching its direction rather than dropped, and a day with no punches still exports a well-formed file. Verified live in the browser on the running install: the sidebar shows Attendance Logs under Attendance Report, the grid heading reads 'Attendance status 2026-09-21 -> 2026-09-23', and the LOG column renders a button on every row.

title: Attendance Logs: Reporting Manager fills in, Log moves last, Edit for a deciding role
detail:
Four follow-ups on the Attendance Logs screen.

1. TEAM LEADER WAS BLANK ON EVERY ROW, and the cause was `??`. attendanceLookups() maps a team with no leader_id to an EMPTY STRING, not null, so the old `?? trim($employment['team_leader'])` chain saw a value, stopped, and printed nothing — silently skipping its own fallback. `??` asks 'is it missing'; the question was 'is it useful', which is `?:`.

2. The owner then settled what the column should mean: the hierarchy is Employee -> Team Lead -> Manager -> Director and EVERY step of it is reporting_manager_id ('the Team Lead is configured the Reporting Manager'), and he asked for the heading to read Reporting Manager 'for more clarity for entire employee list'. So the column is relabelled and the resolution order flipped to put the reporting line FIRST — a column headed 'Reporting Manager' must not quietly print a team's leader instead. Teams and the legacy text column stay on as fallbacks for a tenant who does use the register. Extracted as AttendanceReport::reportingManagerOf() so the precedence has a name and a test rather than a long comment on an inline ternary. NO designation name is tested anywhere: 'Team Lead' is a word this tenant chose for a job, not one the file may know (Law 1).

3. `logs` moved to the END of the declared columns in config/attendance-report.json. Order comes from declaration order and a tenant's saved choice is a SET of codes, never an order — so moving the entry moves the column for everyone, including installs that have already configured their columns. Actions belong at the end of a row.

4. An EDIT button beside Log, linking to that person's Attendance screen where a punch is actually regularised. Asked for as 'Manager, HR Manager and Company Admin'; written as the PERMISSION those roles hold ($mayRate — attendance.regularisation.review or leave.request.decide), never as a list of role names, so a client who renames the job or adds a fourth role changes nothing here. Shown on every row including days with no punch at all: that is precisely the day somebody needs to fix, so gating it on the punch string would hide it exactly when it is wanted.
found: The Team Leader column had never worked on this install — `??` against an empty string, not missing data. Worth remembering as a shape: every ?? in this codebase against a lookup that returns '' for 'not set' is the same latent bug.

config/attendance-report.json already declares a separate strict `reporting_manager` column. On an install whose hierarchy IS the reporting line the two now print the same name, so both carry a note saying pick one.
got_wrong_first: Built the fallback with the teams register FIRST (team leader, then legacy text, then reporting manager), which was right while the column said 'Team Leader' and wrong the moment it said 'Reporting Manager' — it would have shown a team's leader under a heading promising the reporting manager. Flipped, and the test now pins the order rather than the values.
checks: php -l on both changed PHP files; the JSON re-parses; the app.php diff removes exactly the one line it replaces. tests/attendance_log_csv_test.php is now 14 assertions and covers the precedence in both directions plus the empty-string-not-null trap that caused the blank column. Shift needs no change: it is already declared immediately after Date, so it appears there the moment it is ticked — this install has a SAVED column choice, which overrides the shipped default entirely.

title: Attendance Logs: Shift is not the tenant's to drop, Log opens a dialog, Edit raises a regularization
detail:
1. SHIFT WOULD NOT APPEAR however often it was asked for, and the cause is structural rather than a missing tick. A saved column choice is a snapshot of the columns that existed the day somebody pressed Save, and NOTHING reconciles it afterwards — so a column added or promoted later is invisible to every tenant who has ever opened the Columns screen, and they cannot even tick it, because the list they saved is what the screen shows them. columns() now honours an "always": true flag that beats a saved choice, and `shift` carries it. Justified rather than convenient: Late By, Early Exit and Overtime on the same row are ALL measured against the shift, so a row without it says 'late by 42' and never says late for what. Used sparingly — it overrides somebody's explicit choice, which has to be earned.

2. LOG NOW OPENS A DIALOG instead of navigating. New GET `?r=day-log&code=&date=` echoes just the punch table and exits; one <dialog> on the page is filled from it on click. A <dialog> because the browser already does the modal, backdrop, Escape and focus trap. 1,101 rows means pre-rendering a dialog per row was never on the table. The button's href is still the full-page drill, so it works before the script loads and with scripting off; the fetch is the upgrade. Each open takes a ticket so that clicking three rows quickly does not let the slowest response win the dialog.

3. EDIT NOW GOES TO ATTENDANCE REGULARIZATION, not the general attendance sheet: `?r=attendance-corrections&raise=1&emp=&date=`, with the employee selected, the SHIFT OF THAT DAY resolved (not today's), and check-in/check-out prefilled to that shift's start and end. The code from the URL is honoured only when it is in $corrDecidable — the same list the picker offers — so a code typed into the address bar selects nobody the viewer could not already choose. Prefilled, never submitted.
found: The saved-column-choice snapshot problem is general, not a Shift problem: any column this project adds from now on is invisible to every already-configured tenant unless it is marked `always` or the tenant re-saves. Worth a real reconciliation if it bites a third time.
got_wrong_first: Put the new GET fragment handler in among the other action handlers — which sit inside `if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST')`, a block running from line 3141 to 8065. It was dead code on the exact request type it exists to serve, and it lints perfectly. Found by tokenising the file to locate the enclosing block's real close rather than eyeballing the indentation; moved out to file scope after that block.
checks: php -l on both PHP files, JSON re-parses, and the app.php diff removes only the 14 lines it replaces. The POST-guard escape was verified with PHP's own tokeniser, not by reading. attendance_log_csv_test still 14 green. NOT verified in the browser this time: the Chrome tab group dropped twice mid-check, so the dialog, the prefilled regularization form and the Shift column need a human click-through.

title: Raising a regularization fatalled AFTER saving it — $audit refused a MySQL int id
detail:
`$regularisation->request()` returns the new row; `$r['request']['id']` is a native int on MySQL (BIGINT through PDO); the `$audit` closure declared `?string $entityId`; strict_types refuses to coerce. TypeError, fatal page — AFTER the correction row had already been written. That is the worst shape this failure takes: it reads as 'nothing happened' and that is not true, so the next thing somebody does is raise it again.

FIXED AT THE DEFINITION, not the call site: `$audit` now takes `int|string|null` and casts inside, so `$trail->record()` still gets the `?string` it declares and null still means 'no entity' rather than ''. 99 call sites; every one of them was one MySQL int away from the same fatal.

This is the SECOND time this exact bug has been fixed in this file and the first fix is why the second was needed: the leave-request call site carries `(string) $requested['id']` and a comment describing the TypeError precisely — patched there, and only there, leaving the closure `?string` and every sibling caller live. Raising a regularization found it again months later with the same stack trace and a different table. The cast is kept (harmless, and it names the column) with its comment corrected so it no longer claims $audit rejects an int.
found: The codebase already solved this once, three functions below $audit: e() was widened to `string|int|float|bool|null` with a docblock saying 'widened rather than fixed at each call site: there are several hundred of them, and the next column MySQL returns as an int would be the same bug again'. $audit is that sentence coming true.

The file store returns every id as a string, so none of this is reachable in development. It appears only against a real schema — the same shape as the emp_code/gross/joined_on column defects Employment::PORTED documents.
got_wrong_first: The bug is not mine, but MY change is why it fires on the default path. Before the Edit button prefilled check-in/check-out, both fields were blank, the `if ($crDt === '') continue;` loop body never ran, no request was created and the audit line was never reached — you only hit it if you typed times yourself. Prefilling made the fatal the NORMAL outcome of pressing Request. A latent bug plus a convenience is how a convenience gets blamed.
checks: php -l clean; the diff replaces 6 lines and adds the widened signature. Reproduced the exact reported TypeError in isolation under declare(strict_types=1) — 'Argument #3 ($id) must be of type ?string' — and confirmed the widened signature accepts int 3 as '3', a string unchanged, and null as null rather than ''. NOT clicked through in the browser: the Chrome tab group has been dropping, so the owner should re-try Request once.

title: The Log dialog was quieter than the engine: outside-window punches, the real shift, and a row for a day with nothing to punch
detail:
Owner asked whether the dialog's table lists every IN and OUT. Reading DaySettlement to answer turned up that it did not, and two more things beside it.

1. THERE IS A THIRD BUCKET. DaySettlement splits punches into `sessions` (paired), `unpaired` and `outsideWindow`. The dialog and the CSV rendered the first two. ShiftWindow::assign() keeps the third ON PURPOSE and says why in terms: 'A punch outside the window is NOT dropped: it comes back in `outside`... Silently discarding a swipe is how somebody's overtime disappears.' The engine kept them and the report threw them away again one layer up — the same disappearance, one storey higher. day() now returns `outside_window`, and both the dialog and dayCsv() list them, marked and explicitly not counted. Most are honest (a cross-midnight shift puts yesterday's late punch here and settles it on yesterday); the ones that matter are punches no window covers, a 04:00 swipe on a 09:00-18:00 day, which were visible NOWHERE.

2. THE SHIFT COLUMN WAS THE SAME STRING ON EVERY ROW. daily() stamped the caller's `$shiftLabel` — built once from the working calendar's default — onto all 1,101 rows, while muster() beside it has always resolved each employee's real shift and SETTLED the day against it. So a night-shift employee's row was settled 22:00-07:00 and captioned 09:00-18:00, and the Late By next to it read like an error in the figure rather than in the caption: the report disagreeing with itself in two adjacent columns. New shiftLabelFor() resolves per employee-DAY (a roster can move somebody mid-week) and prints the code first — 'GEN · 09:00-18:00' — because the code is the word people say and the times are what a first-time reader needs.

3. A DAY WITH NOTHING TO PUNCH IS STILL A ROW (owner). Weekly off, approved leave and absence used to render as the sentence 'No punch was recorded on this day.' below an empty table. Now the table always has a row carrying the status badge and the rule's own reason, because that is where somebody is already looking. The status comes from the same rule engine the payslip reads, so the row and the pay for that day cannot disagree.
found: The Shift column has been wrong for every non-default-shift employee since the daily view existed, and it is the kind of wrong that discredits the correct column beside it.
got_wrong_first: Nearly answered 'yes, it lists every punch' from the shape of the dialog code. Opening DaySettlement and then ShiftWindow to check is what found the third bucket — the answer was 'almost', and 'almost' on an attendance log is a missing swipe. Also wrote the new CSV assertion without the quoting fputcsv applies to a value containing spaces, so it failed on the first run against correct output.
checks: php -l on both files; app.php diff removes 3 lines, AttendanceReport 1 — only what was replaced. tests/attendance_log_csv_test.php now 15 assertions, green, including one pinning that an outside-window punch reaches the export marked and uncounted. Shift `code`/`name` columns confirmed present in the shifts table (2026_02_01_000400). NOT clicked through: the Chrome tab group has been dropping, so the owner should open one Log dialog on a weekly-off day and one on a night-shift employee.

title: Leave on somebody else's behalf, scoped — and Scope::covers() is one level, not a tree
detail:
Owner asked for: apply leave for team members; managers see only their hierarchy; HR Manager / HR Admin / Branch Admin / Company Admin see everyone; picking somebody shows THAT person's balances; an employee sees only their own; a person with reports gets a Team View table of every member's balance by type.

MOST OF IT ALREADY WORKED. `?r=leave&id=<employment>` has always opened anyone's balances and apply form, guarded by $scope->covers($id, $may('leave.balance.view_others')). What was missing was a way to GET there: you had to leave for the Employees list and come back. So the new work is a scoped picker, not a second leave screen.

New leaveActableFor() builds the candidate list the way regularisationDecidable() does — the whole scope for a role holding `leave.balance.view_others`, plus hierarchyBelow() for a manager who holds none — and no role NAME appears in code; which roles hold the permission is the tenant's answer on Roles & Permissions (Law 1).

The picker renders ABOVE the 'do you have an employee record' split, deliberately: an administrator with no record of their own still has a team to apply for, and the screenshot that prompted this showed a page offering only 'create your own record' to somebody whose whole job there is other people's leave.

New route `leave-team`: employees down, leave types across, available balance in each cell. Columns are the UNION of types across the team because types are scoped per company/branch/designation — building the header from the first row would silently drop a type somebody else is entitled to. A member not entitled to a type gets an em dash, which is a different statement from a zero balance.
found: Scope::covers() reaches `direct_reports` — ONE level — and says so deliberately: 'A skip-level manager therefore does NOT see their reports' reports, which is the safe direction to be wrong in.' hierarchyBelow(), which Attendance Regularization uses, walks the WHOLE tree. Those two disagree, and the leave guard is covers(). So the picker now puts every candidate to the same question the screen will ask, and cannot list anybody the guard would refuse.

That means 'their respective hierarchy' currently means DIRECT reports for leave. Skip-level is a deliberate policy change — DataScope::of('reporting_tree', depth: n), which Scope's own docblock already sketches — and not something a leave picker gets to decide.
got_wrong_first: Built the picker straight from hierarchyBelow() and was about to ship it. It would have listed a skip-level manager's whole sub-tree and then answered 'They do not report to you' on click — a menu of things that do not work, which reads as a broken screen rather than a boundary. Caught by reading Scope::covers() before committing rather than assuming it matched. Also dropped the asort() while rewriting the function and shipped a fifty-name dropdown in store order for about a minute.
checks: php -l clean; the diff removes exactly one line (a `?>` absorbed into the new block). NOT browser-verified — the Chrome tab group has been dropping all session. The important behaviours to click: an administrator with no employee record sees the picker at all; a manager's picker lists their direct reports and nobody deeper; an ordinary employee with no reports sees no picker; Team view totals match what the single-employee screen shows.

title: The reporting line is the whole line: Scope moved from direct_reports to reporting_tree
detail:
Owner, in his own shape: "user 1 reports to user 2; user 2 reports to user 3; user 3 reports to user 4. user 2 should be able to see leaves of user 1; user 3 should see user 2 and user 1; user 4 should see user 3, user 2 and user 1... This should be applicable the entire application wide for any such hierarchy - approvals, leaves, regularizing attendance, etc." Then, when asked: "this is how the actual hierarchy follows in any organization" and "This tree level should be application wide for all the activities, tasks, approvals for everything".

ONE METHOD, ONE LINE OF POLICY. Scope::scope() returned DataScope::of('direct_reports', includeSelf: true) and now returns DataScope::of('reporting_tree', includeSelf: true, depth: DataScope::MAX_REPORTING_DEPTH). Nothing was added to DataScope: it already takes a depth, already walks SubjectContext::managerChain and already raises on a cycle (R-XXII-044). The actual work was subject() — it used to hand the platform ONE link (the subject's immediate manager) and now hands it the whole chain, which is what reporting_tree reads.

New private managerChain(): walks reporting_manager_id upward, immediate manager first, bounded by MAX_REPORTING_DEPTH (12) and memoised per request because only() calls covers() once per row and each link is a store read — a fifty-person list would otherwise walk fifty chains of twelve.

NO CYCLE GUARD IN THE WALK, deliberately, and the test pins it: a cycle fills the chain with repeats and DataScope::reaches() raises on exactly that. Breaking the loop early on a repeat would hide a data defect from the one component whose job is to report it, and a hierarchy quietly missing a level is worse than one that says so. The depth bound alone stops the walk.

WHY THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE IT HAD TO CHANGE: Scope is the single answer to 'whose row is this?'. Leave, leave approvals, attendance regularisation, the attendance report, payslips and every picker narrowed by only() all route through covers() or only(). They moved together, which is the whole reason the class exists — and also why this is the file to be careful in: there is no second place to fix.
found: The previous entry's correction ('Scope::covers() is direct_reports by design, so "their hierarchy" means DIRECT reports for leave') is now superseded. It was an accurate description of the code and the wrong policy. The leave picker written against it needs no change: leaveActableFor() filters candidates through $scope->covers(), so widening covers() widens the picker by construction.

hierarchyBelow(), which Attendance Regularization already used, walks the whole tree. It and covers() disagreed; they agree now, and covers() is the stricter of the two only in that it also demands the permission.
includeSelf stays true: a manager is also a person with their own payslip, and 'sees the team' must not mean 'stops seeing themselves'.
got_wrong_first: Nothing shipped wrong, but the harness lied twice before it told the truth. Its autoloader checked the device's OLD Scope.php before the modified copy, so the skip-level assertions failed against code that already had the fix; flipping the search order fixed that. Then the cycle assertion failed with 'Class ScopeResolutionFailed not found' — a harness gap, not a defect, fixed by staging the file. Worth recording because both looked exactly like a real failure.
checks: New tests/scope_reporting_tree_test.php — 19 assertions, auto-discovered by tests/run.php (glob of tests/*_test.php). Against the NEW Scope: 19 passed, 0 failed. Against the OLD one: 13 passed, 6 FAILED — '3 sees 1 (SKIP-LEVEL, the whole point)', '4 sees 2', '4 sees 1', both only() assertions, and the cycle raise. That old-vs-new split is the proof the change is real rather than a test written to agree with itself. An authorisation WIDENING is the direction that needs a test rather than a look, so every assertion that passes because somebody is now visible has a sibling asserting somebody is still not: never upward (1 does not see 2 or 4), never sideways (3 does not see an unrelated line), and an unbound account still reaches nobody. php -l clean; committed and verified byte-exact against a re-stage. NOT browser-verified — no device shell in this session and the Chrome tab group has been dropping all day.

title: Branch and Reporting Manager are mandatory — form, sheet and the register that decides
detail:
Owner: "While adding an employee through Add Employee form or sample file upload, ensure selecting the Branch and Reporting Manager mandatory. This will help in having proper hierarchy up to date. Later if Branch or reporting manager changes, it can be edited from the Directory." Straight after the reporting-tree change, and for the same reason: a tree is only as good as the lines in it.

WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE: Employee Fields already carries both fields with a `required` flag per field, already drives the Add form, self-onboarding AND the bulk upload sample from one list, and the three screens already put `required` on the input. So this is not a new rule, it is an existing rule that reached exactly one of the ways a value arrives.

THREE EDITS.

1. config/employee-fields.json: "required": true on branch_id and reporting_manager_id.

2. EmployeeFields::sections() now reads `required` from the CATALOGUE as well as from `core` and the tenant's saved tick. It had to be a third source: `core` also means "cannot be turned off", a different promise; and the saved selection is a SNAPSHOT of the screen at the moment Save was pressed, so flipping the catalogue alone would have reached a brand-new tenant and nobody else. Same trap the attendance report's columns sprang last round, second sighting in two days.

3. Enforcement on the server, because `required` was an HTML attribute and nothing else. employeeFieldProblems() in app.php now refuses a required field POSTED BLANK — serving the Add form, Edit and HR's half of an onboarding approval — while still ignoring a field ABSENT from the request, which is how self-onboarding splits the register in two. EmployeeImport::parse() refuses a CREATE row missing a required value, including when the column is not in the sheet at all: the per-cell loop only visits columns the file carries, so a sample with Branch deleted would otherwise have imported a whole organisation with no branches. Update and skip rows are exempt — a correction file carries only the column it corrects.

The bulk sample's LABEL row now marks a required column with ' *'. The code row beneath it is untouched, because that is what the import matches on. Header detection strips non-alphanumerics, so the asterisk changes nothing there.
found: employeeFieldProblems() skipped every blank value with a `continue` before looking at anything, so no required check could ever have fired through it. The HTML attribute was the only thing holding the line on three screens and nothing at all on the fourth path.

Making the two fields required BREAKS FIXTURES, and that is the change working. tests/employee_import_test.php went 42/0 -> 31/11 because its sample CSVs create employees with no branch. Updated the fixtures (not the assertions) and it is 42/0 again — same count, so nothing was weakened to make it pass.

PRE-EXISTING FAILURE, not mine: tests/employee_fields_test.php has one failing assertion, 'field role names a control the form can render'. It fails identically against the unmodified code. Worth a look on the Laragon machine, where the whole suite can run.
got_wrong_first: Wrote the new test against invented fakes (FakeRowStore, FakeEmployeeFields) before reading how this suite actually tests the importer: real Store in a temp dir, real EmployeeFields off the real config. Rewrote it on that pattern. Also nearly shipped without running the EXISTING import test, which the config change breaks by design — a green new test says nothing about the ones already there.
checks: New tests/employee_required_fields_test.php, 20 assertions: 20 passed / 0 failed against the new code, 10 passed / 10 FAILED against the old. tests/employee_import_test.php back to 42/0 with updated fixtures. employee_fields_test unchanged at 253/1 (that 1 is pre-existing). php -l clean on all three PHP files, JSON valid. All six files committed and verified byte-exact against a re-stage. NOT browser-verified.

title: A leave request now says whose it is — identity, hierarchy-scoped filters and export
detail:
Owner, of the Requests table on ?r=leave: "this is an error - it doesn't have the Employee ID and name, Name, company, branch, department and reporting manager who has applied this leave?" Then: "add filters of all Company, Branch, Roles, Designation, Employee to view the leave status / It should also have Export option available". Then: "All these to be available only for the employee to whom other people reports to and follow the hierarchy as mentioned earlier" and "I mean hierarchy tree based".

IDENTITY. New employeeOrgLine(): company, branch, department, designation and who they report to, in one line. The reporting manager comes from AttendanceReport::reportingManagerOf() rather than a second read of reporting_manager_id here — that method already knows the fallback order and already knows a team with no leader resolves to an EMPTY STRING, which is the bug that printed the column blank last round. On ?r=leave it goes in the Requests card header, not a column: every row there belongs to ONE person, so a column would repeat the same value down the table while the page title sits scrolled off the top, which is exactly what the owner was looking at. On Leave Approvals it replaces the shorter designation/department/branch note on both tables, adding company and the reporting manager.

FILTERS. orgFilterBar()/orgFilterOptions()/orgFilterApply() — the same helpers the muster and the directory use, so ORG_FILTERS decides the order app-wide and this bar cannot drift. Company, Branch, Department, Role, Designation, Team, Employee, each with ALL.

THE OPTIONS ARE BUILT FROM THE PEOPLE ALREADY IN THE QUEUE, never from the employees table, and that is the owner's hierarchy instruction taken literally. leaveQueueFor() has already put every one of them through Scope, so the branches and names offered are only the ones this person may open. Building the dropdown from the organisation would hand a manager every branch in the company and then show an empty table for each — a broken-looking screen, and an org chart leaked through a filter box.

EXPORT. New `leave-status-csv` action, one per table (waiting / decided). It rebuilds its rows through the SAME leaveQueueFor() and the SAME orgFilterApply() the screen used, never a query of its own; the columns are the ones the owner listed. Gated on the same test as the screen.

THE TREE, IN THE QUEUE ITSELF. leaveQueueFor() decided 'is this my report?' with `$emp['reporting_manager_id'] === $own` — one level, written inline, and therefore completely unaffected when Scope was widened to the reporting tree this morning. It now asks Scope. That is the second half of "hierarchy tree based": widening Scope was necessary and was not sufficient, because a comparison written inline is exactly the thing a central widening cannot reach.
found: The inline one-level test in leaveQueueFor() is the shape to hunt for elsewhere: any `=== $own` or `reporting_manager_id` comparison written at a call site is a private copy of an authorisation rule and will not follow Scope. hierarchyBelow() and Scope::covers() now agree; inline comparisons are the remaining disagreement.

hasDirectReports() is still one level and is still CORRECT for what it gates ('is this person an approver at all'): anybody with a descendant necessarily has a direct report, so the tree adds nothing to that question. Left alone deliberately.

The filter bar is rendered INSIDE the `$laIsApprover` branch. Somebody nobody reports to already sees 'there is nothing for you to approve'; a row of Company/Branch/Designation dropdowns above that message would contradict it and offer a way to browse an organisation they have no queue in.
got_wrong_first: Left a dead assertion in the new test — a duplicated `same([], ...)` with a dangling `=== null` — which failed and read like a real defect in the self-approval path for a minute. Also nearly shipped the test as a harness-only file: tests/run.php globs tests/*_test.php and requires them with the plain bootstrap, which has no leaveQueueFor(), so it would have fatalled the whole suite. The test now slices the function out of public/app.php itself.
checks: New tests/leave_queue_tree_test.php, 12 assertions, self-contained (it slices leaveQueueFor() out of the live public/app.php and evals it, so it tracks the real function rather than a copy): 12 passed / 0 failed against the new code, 9 passed / 3 FAILED against the old — the three being exactly '3 sees 1', '4 sees three levels down' and the self-approval queue. Negative half included: never upward, never an unrelated line, never your own request, an unbound account has nothing to approve, and the permission route unchanged. leave_approvals_test 7/0, regularisation_hierarchy_test 4/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0, employee_required_fields_test 20/0, employee_import_test 42/0. php -l clean; both files committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified.

title: Leave Approvals as a real table — one column per fact, one row per request; and the picker opens on None
detail:
Owner, of the identity column shipped an hour earlier: "should not combine the other field values along with employee ID and name... company, Branch, Designation, reporting to... all these should be in separate columns for more clarity. Format the page accordingly to avoid overlap and fit in single row view." And: "Asked for can be removed as it is redundant." Then, of the Leave screen: "Apply leave for should have None in the dropdown list. Only if any employee name is selected, the blue Apply leave button should be visible else it should be invisible if None is selected. By default None should be the selection."

HE WAS RIGHT AND THE SCREENSHOT SHOWED WHY. Five values joined with dots, in a column sized for a name, wrapped into a fifteen-line cell and made one request as tall as the screen. A table cannot be sorted, scanned down or exported by a field glued to four others. So employeeOrgLine() became employeeOrgCells(), returning the five separately, and both Leave Approvals tables now carry Emp ID | Name | Company | Branch | Department | Designation | Reporting to as their own columns — the SAME columns in the SAME order on the waiting queue and the decided dashboard, because two tables on one screen describing the same people differently is how somebody reads the wrong row.

SIXTEEN COLUMNS DO NOT FIT A LAPTOP, and the answer is sideways scrolling inside the card (.table-wrap already does it) rather than wrapping every cell: `white-space:nowrap` on the table, lifted only for the two prose columns (Reason, Comments), which get a max-width to wrap inside.

"Asked for" is gone. It printed the requested span and day count immediately beside the From / To / Days columns carrying the same three facts — the only difference being that it showed the pre-edit values, which the audit trail keeps anyway.

employeeOrgLine() survives for the ?r=leave card header, where one person is being described rather than many tabulated, and is now a one-liner over employeeOrgCells().

PERFORMANCE, CAUGHT WHILE SPLITTING: resolving a reporting manager needs every employment's label, and the first version built that map inside the row loop — a fifty-request queue meant fifty passes over the employees table. Now attendanceLookups() is built once per screen (and once per export file) and passed in; new employmentLabels() is the map, which three places were building by hand.

THE PICKER OPENS ON NONE. The empty option used to mean "myself", so there was no way to select nobody and the page always had somebody's apply form open — for HR, a colleague's, one mis-click from a leave request nobody made. None is now an option with the empty value, Myself is an option of its own with a real id, and own-by-default survives exactly where there is no picker: an ordinary employee is offered no choice, so opening Leave still opens their own. With None selected nothing loads, so the blue Apply leave button is simply not there, which is what the owner asked for.
found: Two different nothings on ?r=leave and they must not share a message: 'nobody is picked yet' versus 'your login has no employee behind it'. Telling a linked administrator their account is unlinked because they have not chosen yet sends them to fix something that was never broken. The new empty state asks for own() as well as the picker, so an account that genuinely is unlinked still gets the link card with the picker above it — yesterday's fix intact.

$lvPicker is `$lvActable !== []`, NOT `|| own() !== null`. The first draft had the latter and it would have given every ordinary employee a two-item dropdown defaulting to None — a screen that used to just show them their own leave.
got_wrong_first: First draft of the empty state swallowed the link-your-account card for an administrator with no employee record — the exact screen that was fixed yesterday, undone within a day by a condition that asked only whether the picker existed. Caught by walking the four account shapes (plain employee / linked manager / picked / unlinked admin) through the branch by hand rather than reading it once.
checks: php -l clean. A static th/td count over all 101 tables in app.php: both leave tables balance at 16 and 16 (the pre-existing mismatches elsewhere are multi-row templates, untouched). leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0, leave_approvals_test 7/0, employee_required_fields_test 20/0, employee_import_test 42/0, regularisation_hierarchy_test 4/0. Committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified — this is a layout change and wants a look at a real queue.

title: Probation moves to Companies — one policy per company, colour-coded, inherited until it isn't
detail:
Owner: "Move Probation Settings to Organization Configuration - Companies. The probation settings to be part of Company table. Include the Probation section and have it part of each company added and for the previously added companies, give option to edit this setting. For each company configured, keep them in a separate section with different color coded box. If another new company is added, keep that in another box below that."

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE SCREEN: a group running three companies runs three probation policies, and one tenant-wide number being right for all of them is somebody being confirmed on the wrong day. So this is a data change with a screen on top, not a screen move.

THREE LAYERS: the declared defaults in config/probation.json, then the tenant's saved answer, then the company's. config(?string $companyId) merges them; configFor(array $employment) resolves an employee's company for callers that have a row rather than an id.

INHERITANCE IS LIVE, NOT A COPY, and that is the assertion worth keeping: a company with no settings of its own follows the default AND KEEPS FOLLOWING IT when the default changes. So nothing is written for a company until somebody chooses differently for it, isOverridden() is how the screen tells inherited from set-to-the-same-value, and "Follow the default again" REMOVES the entry instead of writing today's numbers back.

SAVING ONE COMPANY MUST NOT DELETE THE OTHERS. saveRaw() writes the customisation record whole, so saveConfig() reads-merges-writes: the company map goes under one key inside the single `probation` record (a key per company would have been a separately versioned record each, and no way to read "what does this tenant do" without knowing every company id first).

EVERY READ THAT WAS TENANT-WIDE IS NOW PER EMPLOYEE: board() resolves each row's company (one config for the board would have given everybody the first company's end date — a wrong date that looks like a right one), remind() resolves notify_hr / notify_manager / reminder_days / congratulate_employee per employee rather than once for the sweep, and extend() measures "not after the current end" against the employee's own company.

THE SCREEN is appended to the generated Companies module screen rather than built into the module engine, whose whole value is not knowing about any particular table. A default box first, then one box per company in register order, each with a left border and tint derived from crc32 of the company id — stable across loads and machines, and no colour column for somebody to leave unset. A company added on the form above gets its own box on the next load, which is the owner's "another box below that", without anything being created for it. The module that carries the section is named in config/probation.json (`settings_module`), not compared as a literal in the template.

The old Settings card on the Probation board is now a pointer, not a second copy of the form — a duplicate is always the one somebody edits after the real one has moved on.
found: PRE-EXISTING DEFECT the new test surfaced: clearing the Reminder milestones box saved a single same-day reminder instead of being refused. preg_split('/[\s,]+/', '') gives [''], intval('') is 0, and 0 is a valid milestone meaning "the day itself" — so the "at least one milestone" guard could never fire on a blank box. Any non-numeric typing did the same: "soon" became 0. The pieces are now filtered to whole numbers BEFORE they are cast.

Employees with no employer_company_id still exist (records imported before the column was made mandatory earlier today) and get the tenant default rather than a crash — pinned by a test row with no company.
got_wrong_first: Rewrote remind()'s congratulations block with a bad brace balance — caught by php -l, but only because the edit was scripted rather than read back. Also wrote the new test's last two assertions against what the validator SHOULD do rather than what it did, which is how the blank-milestone defect was found; the honest sequence is that the test was wrong first and the code turned out to be wrong too.
checks: New tests/probation_per_company_test.php, 37 assertions, all passing: the shipped default, the tenant default, one company overriding, the OTHERS surviving that save (the Law 3 assertion), two companies at once, live inheritance when the default moves, clearing an override back to the CURRENT default, the board dating three employees by three different rules including one with no company, a company's extra DAYS landing, and both validation guards refusing a per-company save. The existing tests/probation_test.php is unchanged at 26/0 against both old and new. php -l clean, JSON valid, all four files committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified — the colour-coded boxes want a look.

title: Leave Approvals made to fit — tighter cells, clipped values, and a compact view for the last of it
detail:
Owner: "Adjust the formatting of the table to fit the table data in single page view and in single row by removing wrapping the cell values properly." One row per request was already done; the row was still far wider than a screen and only eleven of sixteen columns fitted.

THE PADDING WAS THE BIGGEST WASTE, and it was invisible: the stock cell is 13px/18px, which across sixteen columns is 576px of nothing but padding. This table now pays its own rate — 6px/7px, 12.5px text, smaller decide icons, narrower date and comment inputs.

LONG VALUES ARE CLIPPED, NOT WRAPPED AND NOT DROPPED. Each org cell carries its full value in `title`, so hovering shows it, and the CSV export is untouched. Clipping is only honest while the whole value is one hover and one export away; both are. The five org cells are also now written as a foreach rather than five near-identical lines, so they cannot drift apart one careless edit at a time.

AND THEN THE HONEST PART: no amount of packing makes sixteen columns of real content fit, because two date pickers and a comment box have a floor — Chrome will not render dd-mm-yyyy under about 105px, so ~330px of every row is fixed whatever else is trimmed. The last of the fit is therefore a COLUMN CHOICE, offered as a Compact checkbox that hides Company, Department and Designation: the three that are the same on nearly every row of one manager's queue. Branch and Reporting to stay, because those are the two that differ and the two somebody checks before approving.

It is a VIEW, not a setting — remembered per person in localStorage, nothing saved for the tenant, the cells stay in the DOM with their hover text, and the export is unaffected. Both reads and the write are wrapped in try/catch: localStorage throws in a private window and comes back empty after a clear, and the checkbox has to work either way.
found: Wrote the smaller .la-ico rule ABOVE the existing 34px one, where equal specificity means it would have been silently ignored. Same trap as the dark-mode card headers earlier today, second time in one day. Moved below it with a comment saying why. Worth a habit: an override added to an existing inline <style> goes at the END of it, not next to the thing it is about.
got_wrong_first: Estimated the packed width at ~1300px and nearly shipped that as 'fits', when the owner's own screenshot shows about 1140px of content beside the sidebar. Measured the floor properly instead — the date inputs — and concluded the remaining gap cannot be closed by CSS, which is what turned this from more squeezing into a column choice. Also patched the cell markup with a script whose em dash was written as — while the file holds the literal character; the assertion caught it before anything was written.
checks: A static th/td count over the two leave tables, counting the foreach as the five cells it renders: 16 headers and 16 cells each, with exactly 3 marked hideable in each head and the matching rule on the cells. php -l clean. leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, probation_per_company_test 37/0, probation_test 26/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0. Committed and verified byte-exact on the second attempt (the first commit silently no-oped again). NOT browser-verified — this is a layout change and the fit wants measuring on his actual screen.

title: Probation becomes real columns on companies — one policy, two screens, double-ruled boxes
detail:
Owner: "Include this Probation along with the Companies itself as we have other settings of the companies including time zone, etc. Have proper double line rounded square box around each of the company." Asked where the settings should actually live, he chose columns AND the boxes.

THE RISK IN "BOTH" IS TWO PLACES TO CHANGE ONE NUMBER, so they were made ONE place: the columns are the single source of truth, and the boxes under the Companies list write those same columns. The company's own Edit form and the box are two doors into one row.

NEW MIGRATION 2026_09_23_000100_probation_on_companies: six nullable columns beside `timezone` and `state` — months, days, reminder milestones (a comma-separated list, kept as typed because it is read back into the box it was typed into), and three notify flags. Every one nullable, and NULL IS NOT ZERO: null means "follow the tenant default", 0 in notify_hr means somebody turned HR's reminder off. Defaulting them would have erased that distinction on every company already on file.

`probation_months` IS THE MARKER, not six independent overrides. The form saves all six together, so months set means this company has a policy and months blank means it inherits. Six separate overrides would allow a company with its own reminder days and the tenant's months — a combination nobody chose and nobody could see.

config/modules.json declares the six fields (labels, help) on the companies module, so the module engine renders them on the company's Edit form with no per-module code — the list COLUMNS are left alone, because six more would make that table unreadable and the boxes already show them. Inserted surgically as text: re-dumping the 164KB file through json.dump shrank it to 102KB by reformatting everything, which is churn nobody asked for on a config this size. Verified by parsing both and diffing the structures — only the companies fields differ.

THE OLD PER-COMPANY MAP IS NOW READ-ONLY, a fallback with an end: an install that saved settings before the migration keeps them until that company is saved again, at which point they land in the columns. companyColumnsExist() decides which path a save takes, so the screen works before and after `composer db:migrate`.

THE BOXES: `border:4px double <company colour>` with a 16px radius — border-style: double is a real CSS style, so the two lines are one declaration rather than a wrapper div pretending to be a frame. The DEFAULT box is dashed and grey on purpose: it is not a company, and a box that looks identical to the ones below it is a box somebody eventually types a company's months into. Each company box now also carries that company's code, type, state and time zone on its own line, so it reads as the company's settings with probation among them rather than as a probation form that happens to name a company.
found: The file store's columnsOf() derives columns from the rows it has, so companyColumnsExist() answers correctly on both stores: false on a pre-migration MySQL install (the real column list), true once a row carries the keys. Both paths are covered by the test without mocking either.

Re-serialising a large JSON config to add one key is not a small diff. modules.json is 164KB; json.dump rewrote every line of it. Insert as text against a unique anchor and verify by parsing both sides.
got_wrong_first: Nearly shipped the reformatted modules.json — it parsed, it was valid, and it would have shown up as a 62KB deletion in a diff nobody would read. Also ran a patch script whose first assertion passed and second failed, which left NOTHING written (the file is only written at the end) — worth remembering: a half-applied script here is a not-applied script, and the fix is to re-run the whole thing, not just the failing half.
checks: tests/probation_per_company_test.php now 55 assertions, all passing — the 37 from the customisation path plus 18 for the column path: months/days/milestones/flags read off the row, a 0 flag read as FALSE rather than missing, saveConfig landing in the COLUMN (which is what keeps the box and the Edit form honest), the rest of the company row untouched by a probation save, clearing blanking all six so no half a policy is left behind, an untouched company inheriting, and a save for a company that does not exist refused. probation_test unchanged 26/0. php -l clean, both JSON files valid and structurally diffed against their originals. NOT browser-verified; `composer db:migrate` has NOT been run for the new migration.

title: Probation stops being a section — it is company columns, edited where every other company setting is
detail:
Owner: "Probation should be within each company box, not separately and these columns should also be part of the Companies table itself." Right on both counts, and the answer was mostly DELETION.

The six are already real columns on `companies` (2026_09_23_000100) and already declared as fields on the companies module. What was still wrong was that the screen kept a second editor for them below the list, which is a second place to change one number — the exact thing the columns were meant to end.

SO: the six are added to the module's `columns` list, which is what puts them in the Companies table beside Time zone and Status; and the separate Probation section now renders ONLY while `companyColumnsExist()` is false. Once `composer db:migrate` has run, the columns are there, Edit shows them with their labels and help, and the section is gone. Until then it renders with a plain statement of why it is there and that it will disappear — a bridge with an end date rather than a feature.

The Probation board's Settings card was repointed to match: probation is set by editing a company, not by a box under a list, and it names the migration when the install still needs it.
found: The right shape was visible once the columns existed and nobody removed the old editor. A migration that adds columns is only half a move; the other half is deleting whatever was standing in for them, and it is easy to leave that standing because it works.

The Companies list is now thirteen columns wide and will scroll sideways. That is what was asked for, and it is the same trade the Leave Approvals table just made — worth watching whether the six probation columns earn their place there or whether months alone would do.
got_wrong_first: Built the section as the way to edit per-company probation one message before the columns existed, then kept it after they did. It was correct at the time and stopped being correct the moment the migration was written — worth noticing sooner than the owner does.
checks: modules.json parsed and structurally diffed against the original: only the companies module differs, and only its `columns` list. php -l clean. probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0, employee_required_fields_test 20/0. All files committed and verified byte-exact — INCLUDING docs/build-journal.json and docs/heartbeat.json, whose previous commit was confirmed to have silently no-oped (the device had dropped before the usual re-stage check, and the check on reconnection found both still carrying the older state). The re-stage-and-cmp habit earned its keep again.

title: The Companies screen becomes one box per company, with its settings grouped and colour-coded inside it
detail:
Owner: "remove the probation section from below and for each company, adjust it in proper boxes with single screen view properly; color code Time zone and Probation sub sections appropriately."

THE LOOSE SECTION WAS THE WRONG WAY ROUND. It was a list of forms that each named a company; the company is the thing and its settings belong inside it. So it is gone, and each company is now a box holding sub-sections: WHERE IT IS (code, type, state, time zone, GSTIN, status) and PROBATION (the six, editable in place).

ACCENTS BY MEANING, NOT BY COMPANY. The company's own crc32 colour is its double border; the sub-sections carry the SAME two colours in every box — teal for where it is, violet for probation — so a sub-section is recognisable by colour before it is read. A colour per company per sub-section would have been decoration; one colour per KIND is a legend.

AND IT FITS A SCREEN, which the thirteen-column table did not. The six probation columns are pulled back OUT of the module's list columns (they stay as fields, so the Edit form still carries them), and the two sub-sections sit in `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr))` — side by side where there is room, stacked where there is not, never a row scrolling past the edge. That is the same fit problem the Leave Approvals table had, solved the other way: there, sixteen columns had to stay a row; here the row could become a card.

LABELS COME FROM THE MODULE'S DECLARED FIELDS, read out of $spec — the same source the Edit form uses — so a label changed in config/modules.json changes in both places rather than in one and not the other (Law 1).

The migration banner survives as a line inside the card rather than as a gate on the whole section: the boxes work before `composer db:migrate` (settings are kept beside the record) and after (they are on it), and the card says which.
found: Two screens for one setting is fine when they write the same columns and say so; it is the SECOND STORE that is the defect, not the second door. The box and the Edit form both go through Probation::saveConfig(), so this stays one answer.

The default-probation panel is deliberately NOT one of the bordered company boxes — flat, dashed, neutral. A panel that looks like the company boxes is one somebody eventually types a company's months into.
got_wrong_first: Added the six probation columns to the Companies list table one message earlier because the owner asked for the columns to be 'part of the Companies table'. That read the sentence as being about the table on screen rather than about the database table, and it produced the thirteen-column row he then objected to. The columns are on the `companies` TABLE; they did not need to be on the companies LIST.
checks: php -l clean; the template's if/foreach nesting checked by counting the branch closers around the replaced block (137 lines out, 182 in) as well as by the parse. modules.json parsed and structurally diffed against the original — only the companies module's `columns` differs, its `fields` unchanged. probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0. Both files committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified: this is a layout rewrite and wants a look at a two-company install.

title: One box, every field — the sub-sections were a judgement nobody asked for
detail:
Owner: "Why are you segregating the components? I want each and every field of the company within a SINGLE box."

He is right, and the mistake is worth naming: splitting a company's record into "where it is & time zone" and "probation" was a judgement about which of its own settings belong together, and nothing asked for that judgement. A company has fields. The box shows them.

So the two accented sub-sections are gone, along with $prbSub, $prbPairs, $prbLabel and the two meaning-colours. Each company box is now ONE grid: every declared field, label above value, in columns that fold with the width.

THE FIELD LIST IS THE MODULE'S, not a list typed into the template. $spec is exactly what the Edit form renders — the order config/modules.json declares, with the labels it declares — so a field added there appears in the box with no change to this code, and one removed disappears from both. The previous version named six columns by hand, which is the list that goes stale.

A lookup shows its NAME, a yes/no column shows Yes or No rather than 1 or 0, and an empty one shows an em dash. Same rules the employee export already follows.

WHAT SURVIVES AS A SUB-SECTION, and only until the migration runs: the six probation fields are not columns yet, so Modules::fields() cannot return them (it intersects the declared list with the columns that actually exist) and they cannot be shown or edited as fields. Each box therefore carries one probation form below a dashed rule, labelled "not yet a column on this install", which disappears the moment `composer db:migrate` has run and they join the grid with everything else.
found: Modules::fields() intersecting declared fields with real columns is the reason the pre-migration state is detectable at all — the six simply are not in $spec until the columns exist, so the bridge form's condition is a fact about the database rather than a flag somebody has to remember to flip.
got_wrong_first: Designed the box around what seemed like a sensible grouping instead of around what was asked for. Two messages earlier the ask was 'probation within each company box'; the answer to that was a box per company, not a taxonomy of a company's fields. When a request is about where something lives, moving it is the whole job — adding structure on top is inventing a second request.
checks: php -l clean; no stale references to the removed helpers ($prbSub/$prbPairs/$prbLabel/$prbWhere/$prbHow all gone). probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0. Committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified: wants a look at a two-company install, before AND after the migration, since the bridge form's presence is what changes.

title: The duplicate was mine: the probation section was drawing every company a second time
detail:
Owner: "Why do we see Redundant data again? ... even after hard refresh the same duplicate data remains... what is going on here?" and "If Edit is clicked and nothing changed ... I should be able to just Close the edit box or click Back".

TWO REAL DEFECTS, both introduced by me in the last few rounds, and neither a styling question.

1. THE DUPLICATE. The section below the Companies register had grown into a second rendering of the same rows — first as colour-coded boxes, then as a full field grid per company — sitting directly under the table that already lists them. Every company appeared twice on one screen. It survived a hard refresh because it was not a cache: it was in the page, twice, by construction. REMOVED. What is left is only what exists nowhere else: the TENANT DEFAULT (which belongs to no company, so has no row above), and — only until `composer db:migrate` has run — one compact probation row per company, because until the columns exist Modules::fields() cannot return them and Edit cannot show them. After the migration that goes too and probation is edited with the rest of a company's fields. 214 lines out, 108 in.

2. THE EDIT BOX THAT WOULD NOT CLOSE. There has always BEEN a Cancel — at the bottom of the form, under twenty-odd fields, which on a company is a screen and a half below the heading somebody just clicked. A way out that must be scrolled to is a way out nobody finds. There is now a "Close without saving" beside the title, with a line saying nothing is stored until Save is pressed, so closing IS the revert. The form reopening after a refresh is correct and not a bug: the address carries `&edit=<id>`, so reloading it faithfully reopens it — but that reads as stuck when the only exit is off-screen.
found: A screen that renders the same records twice cannot be fixed by aligning it better. Three rounds were spent on the layout of a section whose real problem was that it should not have existed — the register above was always the list, and Edit was always how a field is changed.

Nearly re-introduced the trap this very file documents: the 'Follow the default' button was written as a second control named `action` inside the form whose hidden input is also named `action`. Both are sent and the server keeps whichever it reads last. Given its own <form> instead.
got_wrong_first: Kept answering 'make the boxes better' when each answer added another copy of the company data. The owner said 'redundant' the moment it appeared and I read it as a layout note. When somebody says they are seeing the same thing twice, the question is what is rendering it twice, not how to arrange it.
checks: php -l clean; no stale references to the removed helpers. probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, scope_reporting_tree_test 19/0, employee_import_test 42/0. Committed and verified byte-exact. Still NOT browser-verified — and on this one that matters more than usual, because the fix is about what is on the screen.

title: Companies stops being a table plus an edit screen: every company IS its own open box
detail:
Owner, after four rounds of me mis-reading him: "You said there is cancel button, it is visible Only to you - not for us (Do not lie)"; "Why do you have table with the company names separately again when I clearly said for Each company, have box type structure with ALL the relevant fields within that box for that particular company. NO Other data outside the box for any company"; "The initial top configuration is default for all"; "I do not want this separate additional box anymore" (crossing out the whole Probation card); "Probation should be there within each company".

HE WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE BUTTON. The original Cancel is `<a class="btn">` with no variant, and `.btn` alone declares no background and no colour — only padding and a radius. It is in the markup and it renders as nothing. I asserted it existed from reading the source instead of reading the STYLESHEET, which is not the same as it being on his screen.

AND RIGHT ABOUT THE SHAPE. A register table plus a separate Add/Edit card is two renderings of the same rows; that is what kept coming back as 'redundant data' however the second one was styled.

SO, FOR A MODULE THAT DECLARES `"boxes": true` (config/modules.json, not a key tested in this template — a register of two companies is sensibly drawn this way and one of four hundred branches is not, and that is the customer's call):
  - the generated list table is NOT DRAWN. Not hidden with CSS, not made smaller: a screen that builds the same rows twice is the defect, whichever copy is on top.
  - every record is its own always-open form, named for the record rather than 'Edit Company #3', with Delete beside the name.
  - so there is nothing to open, nothing to close, and no `&edit=` in the address to survive a refresh. The whole class of 'the edit box will not go away' is gone rather than fixed.
  - Add appends one empty box; a register with nothing in it shows one anyway, because otherwise there is no way to start.

PROBATION IS INSIDE THE BOX, as a separate <form> only because forms cannot nest — and only until `composer db:migrate` runs, after which the six are ordinary fields in the form above, still inside the same box.

THE SEPARATE PROBATION CARD IS DELETED. The tenant DEFAULT moved back onto the Probation board, which is where it belongs: it is the setting that applies when nothing else does — a company that never set its own, and an install with no company added yet — so it has no company box to live in. Its form posts `back=probation` and the handler now returns to whichever screen asked.

The single Add/Edit card still exists for every other module, unchanged, and keeps its Close.
found: `.btn` with no variant class is invisible in this stylesheet: `.btn{display:inline-flex;padding;border-radius;font}` and nothing else — no background, no border, no colour. Any control written as `<a class="btn">` reads as plain text at best. Worth a sweep; the module form's Cancel was one and there are others.
Reading a template and concluding what a person sees is a category error. The button was in the HTML and absent from the screen, and only the CSS says which.
got_wrong_first: Four rounds of restyling a second rendering of the same rows, each time treating 'redundant' as a layout note. And asserting a Cancel button was present when what I had checked was the markup, not the appearance — he was right to call that out.
checks: php -l clean. The boxes region's if/foreach/endif closers counted as well as parsed. probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0, employee_import_test 42/0. app.php and modules.json committed and verified byte-exact. NOT browser-verified — and this one genuinely needs it before anything else is built on top.

title: The boxes attempt is reverted, and the migration used a column type this project does not allow
detail: TWO FAILURES IN ONE ROUND, both mine. 1. THE COMPANIES SCREEN WENT BLANK. The boxes-per-record change suppressed the register table and then drew no boxes: the header still counted 2 records, and nothing below the branding card rendered. Reverted to the table plus the single Add/Edit card. The Close on that form is now `btn btn-outline btn-sm` rather than the bare `btn` that declares no background, border or colour and is therefore invisible — the owner was right that the Cancel he was told about could not be seen. The cause is NOT yet found, and the honest position is that I could not reproduce it: the application only runs on his machine and I was reading source instead of a rendered page. Structural checks all passed — php -l, div nesting (the list card closes at its own and the endif follows it), alt-syntax if/endif balance, and a browser check that showed no PHP error and a page that completes — which is exactly why guessing further was the wrong move. Before this is attempted again the app needs to be stood up somewhere I can watch it render. 2. THE MIGRATION WAS REFUSED BY THE VOCABULARY. `composer db:migrate` died on Blueprint::unsignedSmallInteger(): this project declares the column types it allows in tests/lib/laravel_schema_stub.php and refuses anything else BY NAME rather than accepting it quietly. That guard did its job. Changed to unsignedTinyInteger, which is in the list and tops out at 255 against a form that accepts 1-36 months and 0-30 days — so the narrower type is not a squeeze, and widening the vocabulary for a column that fits the existing one would have been extending a guard to avoid reading it. Nothing was half-applied: months is the first column the loop reaches, so it threw before any ALTER ran.
found: `.btn` with no variant class declares only padding, radius and font in smartprs.css — no background, no border, no colour. Anything written `<a class="btn">` is in the markup and invisible on screen. The module form's Cancel was one. Worth a sweep.

The migration stub is a real gate, not a convenience: it names the unsupported method instead of passing it through. Check tests/lib/laravel_schema_stub.php for the allowed types BEFORE writing a migration — id, foreignId, unsignedBigInteger, unsignedInteger, unsignedTinyInteger, integer, bigInteger, string, char, text, longText, json, boolean, date, dateTime, time, timestamp, decimal, uuid, binary.

A migration can now be run OFFLINE against that same stub — require the stub, Schema::create() the table it alters, call up(), and print Schema::$statements. It prints the exact ALTERs and proves the second run adds nothing. That check takes a minute and would have caught this before it reached his terminal.
got_wrong_first: Shipped a migration without running it, and shipped a screen rewrite without seeing it render — then spent several messages theorising about why the screen was blank instead of restoring the working one. The owner's data was never touched, but he had a broken screen for longer than he should have because I kept debugging instead of reverting.
checks: The migration was run against tests/lib/laravel_schema_stub.php with a companies table present: six ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN statements, the right types (TINYINT UNSIGNED, VARCHAR(120), TINYINT(1)), all NULL, all commented; a second run adds 0 statements. php -l clean on everything. probation_per_company_test 55/0, probation_test 26/0, leave_queue_tree_test 12/0. app.php, modules.json and the migration committed and verified byte-exact.

title: Reporting ring crashed the Directory; the top of the organisation had no truthful answer
detail:
SYMPTOM: ?r=employees fatal — ScopeResolutionFailed access.reporting_cycle_detected for employee 56 (AI2001 ⇄ AIPL-1002 report to each other).

CAUSE, TWO CHANGES COMBINING: (1) 23 Sep made Reporting Manager required on Add AND Edit with no way to say 'nobody', so whoever edited the top person had to pick a subordinate — that made the ring; (2) 24 Sep made the reporting tree apply to every bound account, so the ring was walked on every list and DataScope's (correct) raise escaped Surface\Scope and killed the page — including the edit form needed to fix it.

FIX: Surface\Scope::lineCovers() treats a reporting cycle as a DENIAL of the line (never an allow, never fatal); other ScopeResolutionFailed still rethrows. Directory shows a banner naming each ring (ReportingLines::cycles(), which existed but was never wired). update-employee refuses a manager who already reports up to the employee (reportingLoopVia). Reporting Manager gains a declared none_option (catalogue, not code): 'NONE' / 'No one — top of the organisation' — satisfies required, stored as NULL, offered on the form, in the upload sample dropdown and accepted by EmployeeImport (isNone). Edit form pre-selects it for someone with no manager who has direct reports.

WHAT I GOT WRONG FIRST: the first loop guard read post('reporting_manager_id'); the form posts f_reporting_manager_id, so it never fired. Caught while wiring none_option. And neither 23/24 Sep change was tested against the top-of-org case.

TESTS: new tests/reporting_top_of_org_test.php 14 assertions — 8 pass / 6 fail before, 14 pass after. employee_required_fields still 20/20. composer check NOT run: this session has no shell on the Laragon machine.

title: Probation → confirmation → statutory applicability in payroll
detail:
Reminders to Admin/HR Admin roles (role: recipients, daily sweep, top-bar bell); Confirm/Extend dialog with mandatory remarks and PF/ESI/PT/LWF/TDS answers; confirm sets Employee Type and stage to Permanent; Employee Type blank + required on forms. NEW surface/StatutoryApplicability.php + config/statutory-applicability.json: an explicit No removes that head's components at close, verify, live salary and payslip.

FOUND WRONG: probation reminders were addressed to 'hr', a code no login holds; nothing in payroll read pf_applicable/esi_applicable; the board ignored employment_type.

TESTS: tests/probation_confirmation_test.php 54/54 (includes a real close: PT=No nets exactly ₹200 more, verify reproduces). composer check NOT run (no shell on the Laragon machine).

title: Visibility by reporting line; payroll accuracy; org wiring id-first; dropdowns not free text; role hygiene
detail:
Owner: an Employee/Agent sees only their own data; a manager only their reporting tree; every org field wired, no duplicates, no blanks, no free text; calculations accurate.

BUILT: Scope::LINE (default reach; config/role-reach.json), unlinked logins fail closed, Modules::restrictEmployees for ?r=m lists/lookups/edit/save, module-view-guards.json; requests/KPI/payslip/settlement/payroll/bulk scoped; self-service My Details by id with self_service_excluded. Payroll: govt HRA/PT priced per branch (rule variants in group key and stored for verify), narrowest-scope precedence, employee_status computed, publish refuses rules that would abort the close, department scope, as_closed snapshot for payslip headers, C-/D- prefix fixes. Wiring: orgReconcileEmployees() keeps text in step with ids; surface/OrgRename.php propagates renames into rules/formats/customisations; surface/OrgConsistency.php refuses mismatched company/branch/department/designation/team on Directory and import. Dropdowns: employee_id lookups in every module, module-text-lookups.json, distinct labels, Team vs Department split, hire/transfer by id, payslip designer employee select, attendance shift select. Roles: case-insensitive, canonical session role, mayGrant guard, role rename moves logins/grants. Duplicate registers (leave-types, leaves, salary-components modules) open the real screens.
